kaabu-empire.s: The Kaabu Empire was a Mandinka state in present-day Guinea-Bissau, Senegal and The Gambia. It emerged in the thirteenth century as an outlying province of the Mali Empire and later became independent.

kabongo-luba.s: Kabongo Luba was one of the two states into which the Luba kingdom split after a succession civil war in the late nineteenth century. Its rival was Kasongo Luba.

kabuki.s: Kabuki is a form of Japanese theatre combining drama, music and dance, known for stylised acting and elaborate costumes. It developed in the early seventeenth century and flourished in the urban culture of Edo.

kabul.s: Kabul is a city in present-day Afghanistan, strategically placed on routes between Central Asia and India. Babur, the last Timurid prince expelled from Central Asia, took Kabul and used it as his base.

kaidu.s: Kaidu was a Mongol prince, a grandson of Ögedei, who dominated Central Asia from 1272 to 1301. Allied with Duwa of the Chagatai Khanate, he waged long wars against Kublai Khan and the Yuan Dynasty.

kaifeng.s: Kaifeng is a city in north-central China on the Yellow River plain. It was the capital of the Northern Song and one of the largest and most commercialised cities of its time.

kairouan.s: Kairouan is a city in present-day Tunisia, founded in the seventh century as an early Arab Muslim centre and a seat of religious learning. Around 1040 CE the Gudala chieftain Yahya ibn Ibrahim met the jurist Abu Imran al-Fasi there.

kaiser.s: Kaiser is the German word for emperor, derived from the Roman name Caesar. In the German Empire it was the title of the King of Prussia as German Emperor, first held by Wilhelm I from 1871.

kaiyuan-era.s: The Kaiyuan era was the reign period of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang Dynasty from 713 to 741. It is regarded by Chinese historians as the Tang's cultural and administrative high point.

kalala-ilunga.s: Kalala Ilunga is the figure credited in oral tradition with founding the Second Luba Dynasty around 1585.

kaleb.s: Kaleb was a king of Aksum who reigned c. 514–542 CE.

kalebs-yemen-campaign.s: Kaleb's Yemen campaign was the Aksumite military expedition to South Arabia in the sixth century CE under King Kaleb. It followed the persecution of Christians by the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas and was undertaken in co-operation with the Byzantine Empire.

kalidasa.s: Kalidasa was a classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the language. His works include the drama Abhijnanashakuntalam and the poem Meghaduta.

kalinga.s: Kalinga was an ancient region on the eastern coast of India, roughly corresponding to present-day Odisha. It was conquered by the Maurya emperor Ashoka in a bloody war.

kalinga-war.s: The Kalinga War was the Maurya Empire's conquest of Kalinga under Ashoka, dated on the site to 261 BCE. Ashoka's own edicts record the great loss of life it caused.

kamal-ud-din-behzad.s: Kamāl ud-Dīn Behzād, or Bihzad, was a Persian painter of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, the most celebrated master of the Herat school. He worked under Timurid patronage at the court of Husayn Bayqara.

kamikaze.s: Kamikaze, meaning divine wind, is the Japanese name for the typhoons that destroyed the Mongol invasion fleets sent against Japan by the Yuan Dynasty in the late thirteenth century. The storms helped preserve Japanese independence.

kandahar.s: Kandahar is a city in southern Afghanistan, long contested between Iranian and Indian powers. Under the late Safavid Empire, its Sunni Ghilzai Afghans revolted under Mir Wais from 1704.

kandake.s: Kandake was the title of royal women, often queen mothers or ruling queens, in the kingdom of Kush. Several kandakes held significant political authority and some ruled in their own right.

kanem-bornu-empire.s: The Kanem–Bornu Empire was a long-lived state around Lake Chad, first centred in Kanem and later in Bornu. It was ruled for centuries by the Sayfawa dynasty and was among the earliest states in the region to adopt Islam.

kanesh.s: Kanesh, modern Kültepe in Turkey, was an ancient city in central Anatolia. In the early second millennium BCE it hosted the most important Assyrian merchant colony, or karum.

kangaba.s: Kangaba is a region on the upper Niger in present-day Mali, the original heartland of the Keita dynasty. As the Mali Empire declined, the Keita rulers lost their wider territories.

kangxi-emperor.s: The Kangxi Emperor was one of the longest-reigning rulers in Chinese history, governing the Qing Empire from 1661 to 1722. He suppressed the Revolt of the Three Feudatories and took Taiwan from the Zheng family in 1683.

kaniaga.s: Kaniaga was a region in the western Sahel that was home to the Sosso kingdom, once a vassal of Ghana. Around 1140 the Sosso began subjugating Wagadou, the heartland of Ghana.

kano.s: Kano is a city in northern Nigeria and one of the historic Hausa city-states. Under the Sokoto Caliphate it became the principal commercial centre, famous for its indigo-dyed textiles traded across the Sahara.

kansala.s: Kansala was the capital of the Kaabu Empire in present-day Guinea-Bissau. It was the seat of the Mandinka ruling elite.

kanta-and-balama.s: The kanta and balama were professional military commanders appointed by Askia Muhammad in the Songhai Empire. Each was responsible for a specific territorial zone.

kanun.s: Kanun was the body of secular law issued by Ottoman sultans, alongside Islamic sharia. Suleiman the Magnificent, known as Kanuni or the Lawgiver, systematised it in codes governing criminal justice, land tenure and taxation.

kara-koyunlu.s: The Kara Koyunlu, or Black Sheep Turkomans, were a Turkoman tribal confederation that ruled parts of eastern Anatolia, Azerbaijan, Iraq and western Iran in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. They were rivals of the Aq Qoyunlu.

kara-mustafa-pasha.s: Kara Mustafa Pasha was an Ottoman grand vizier of the late seventeenth century. He led the Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1683, which was broken by a relief army under Jan III Sobieski.

karakorum.s: Karakorum was the capital of the Mongol Empire in central Mongolia, established under Ögedei. It was the seat of the Great Khan.

kardar.s: A kardar was a revenue officer in the administration of the Sikh Empire. Kardars collected land revenue assessed according to cultivation type and yield, through local intermediaries.

karelia.s: Karelia is a region between the Gulf of Finland and the White Sea, divided today between Finland and Russia. Parts of it were held by Sweden in the seventeenth century.

karim-khan-zand.s: Karim Khan Zand was the founder of the Zand dynasty, who ruled most of Iran from Shiraz after the collapse of Afsharid power, and died in 1779. He declined the title of shah and styled himself Vakil, or regent.

karl-i.s: Karl I, or Charles I of Austria, was the last Emperor of Austria and King of Hungary, reigning from 1916 to 1918. He sought a separate peace during the First World War without success.

karluks.s: The Karluks were a Turkic people of Central Asia. In 744 CE, together with the Uyghurs and Basmyls, they seized the Gokturk centre at Ötüken and killed the last Gokturk khagan.

karnak.s: Karnak is a vast temple complex at Thebes, present-day Luxor, dedicated chiefly to the god Amun. It was greatly expanded during the Egyptian New Kingdom, including a major building programme under Hatshepsut, and functioned as a religious and economic centre.

karum.s: A karum was a trading colony or merchant quarter in the ancient Near East. The best-known is Karum Kanesh in Anatolia, the centre of an Assyrian merchant network.

karun-river.s: The Karun River is the largest river in Iran, flowing through Khuzestan into the Shatt al-Arab. Under Shapur I, the Band-e Kaisar dam was built across it near Shushtar, reportedly with the labour and engineering skills of Roman prisoners.

kasai.s: Kasai is a region in the south of the present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo, named after the Kasai River. Lunda expansion under rulers such as the Mwaant Yaav extended the empire north into Kasai.

kasbah-of-the-udayas.s: The Kasbah of the Udayas is a fortress at the mouth of the Bou Regreg river in Rabat, Morocco. It was built up by the Almohads in the twelfth century as part of their development of Rabat.

kashgaria.s: Kashgaria is a historical name for the western Tarim Basin, centred on the oasis city of Kashgar in present-day Xinjiang. It was part of the territories received by Chagatai Khan from the former Qara Khitai realm.

kashmir.s: Kashmir is a mountainous region in the north of the Indian subcontinent, famed for its shawls. Ranjit Singh conquered it for the Sikh Empire, and its revenues and trade were important to the empire.

kashta.s: Kashta was a king of Kush in the eighth century BCE who extended Kushite authority into Upper Egypt. His successor Piye completed the conquest of Egypt.

kasongo-luba.s: Kasongo Luba was one of the two states into which the Luba kingdom divided after a succession civil war in the late nineteenth century. It was named after the claimant Kasongo Nyembo.

kasongo-nyembo.s: Kasongo Nyembo was a claimant to the Luba throne after the death of Ilunga Kabale. His civil war with the rival claimant Kumwimbe Tshimbu split the kingdom into Kasongo Luba and Kabongo Luba.

kassite-dynasty.s: The Kassite dynasty ruled Babylonia for about four centuries after the fall of the First Dynasty of Babylon. It was overthrown around 1158 BCE by the Elamite kings Shutruk-Nahhunte and Kutir-Nahhunte, who carried off monuments such as the Code of Hammurabi to Susa.

kassites.s: The Kassites were a people, probably from the Zagros region, who took control of Babylonia after the Hittite sack of Babylon and ruled it for about four centuries. They adopted Babylonian culture and the cult of Marduk.

kataphraktoi.s: Kataphraktoi, or cataphracts, were heavily armoured cavalry in which both rider and often horse were protected by armour. They were a core element of Parthian and Sasanian armies.

katoikia.s: A katoikia was a Greek or Macedonian military colony in the Hellenistic kingdoms, in which settlers received land in return for military service. The Seleucids founded many such colonies alongside new cities across their domains.

kavad-ii.s: Kavad II was a Sasanian king who deposed and killed his father Khosrow II in 628 CE after the defeat by Heraclius. He made peace with the Byzantines but died within the same year.

kay-tribe.s: The Kayı tribe was a branch of the Oghuz Turks. Ottoman tradition holds that Osman I, the founder of the dynasty, belonged to the Kayı clan.

kazakhs.s: The Kazakhs are a Turkic people of the Central Asian steppe. Their lands were progressively absorbed by the Russian Empire during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

kazallu.s: Kazallu was an ancient city-state in Mesopotamia. According to the site, Babylon was taken from Kazallu around 1894 BCE by the Amorite chieftain Sumuabum, who declared independence and began walling the city.

kazembe.s: Kazembe was a kingdom in the Luapula valley in present-day Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, founded by Lunda chiefs. In the period of their greatest extent, Luba military expeditions extended southward towards Kazembe.

kebek-coin.s: The kebek was a standardised silver coin introduced by Kebek Khan of the Chagatai Khanate in the 1320s. It was so widely trusted that it became the basis of later currency in the region.

kebek-khan.s: Kebek Khan was a ruler of the Chagatai Khanate in the early fourteenth century. In the 1320s he introduced a currency reform with standardised silver coins and tried to establish a settled capital at Qarshi in present-day Uzbekistan.

kebra-nagast.s: The Kebra Nagast, or Glory of the Kings, is an Ethiopian text compiled in Ge'ez in the medieval period. It tells of the Queen of Sheba, King Solomon and their son Menelik I, and the bringing of the Ark of the Covenant to Ethiopia.

kediri-kingdom.s: The Kediri Kingdom was a Hindu-Buddhist state in eastern Java that flourished in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Its rise, followed by that of Singhasari and Majapahit, created a powerful rival centre in the region.

kedukan-bukit-inscription.s: The Kedukan Bukit inscription is a stone inscription dated 682 CE, found near Palembang in Sumatra. Written in Old Malay, it is the earliest surviving example of that language.

keira-dynasty.s: The Keira dynasty was the ruling dynasty of the Darfur Sultanate, founded in the seventeenth century by Sulayman Solong. It ruled until the defeat of Sultan Ibrahim in 1874.

keita-dynasty.s: The Keita dynasty was the ruling Mandinka lineage of the Mali Empire, founded by Sundiata Keita in the thirteenth century. Under rulers such as Mansa Musa it presided over one of the richest states of the medieval world.

kenjutsu.s: Kenjutsu is the Japanese art of swordsmanship. During the long peace of the Edo period, elaborate kenjutsu schools developed, emphasising technique, discipline and ritual.

kente-cloth.s: Kente cloth is a brightly coloured woven textile of the Akan peoples of present-day Ghana, made from interwoven strips of cloth. It was associated with royalty and important occasions.

kerma.s: Kerma is an archaeological site and ancient city in northern Sudan, the centre of a major Nubian kingdom from around 2500 BCE. It was the first centre of the Kushite state before power shifted to Napata and Meroë.

kerman.s: Kerman is a city in south-eastern Iran. In 1794 the last Zand ruler, Lotf Ali Khan, was captured there by Agha Muhammad Khan Qajar after a prolonged siege.

kertanegara.s: Kertanegara was the last king of Singhasari in eastern Java. Around c.

khabur-river.s: The Khabur River is a tributary of the Euphrates in north-eastern Syria. Its valley was the heartland of the Mitanni Empire and its capital Washukanni.

khagan.s: Khagan, also qaghan, was the title of the supreme ruler among the Turkic and Mongol peoples, meaning khan of khans. It was used by the rulers of the Gokturk Empire and the Khazar Khaganate.

khalid-ibn-al-walid.s: Khalid ibn al-Walid was an Arab military commander of the early Islamic period, celebrated as one of the most successful generals of his age. Leading armies for the Rashidun Caliphate, he played a central part in campaigns against the Sasanian Empire in Iraq and the Byzantine…

khalifa.s: Khalifa, rendered in English as caliph, is the Arabic title for the successor to the Prophet Muhammad as leader of the Muslim community. The office emerged after Muhammad's death in 632, when Abu Bakr became the first caliph of the Rashidun Caliphate.

khalsa.s: The Khalsa is the collective body of initiated Sikhs, established by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699 as a community bound by shared discipline, identity and readiness to defend the faith. It provided the ideological and military core from which the Sikh Empire emerged under Ranjit…

khalwa.s: Khalwa refers to the Quranic schools found across the Sudanic belt of Africa, where pupils learned to recite and write the Quran and received basic religious instruction. In the Wadai Empire, a network of khalwa schools provided literacy and Islamic education under the…

khami.s: Khami is an archaeological site in south-western Zimbabwe, known for its terraced dry-stone walls and enclosures. It belongs to the stone-building tradition descended from Great Zimbabwe and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

khanbaliq.s: Khanbaliq, meaning 'city of the khan', was the capital built by Kublai Khan on the site of present-day Beijing. It served as the principal seat of the Yuan Dynasty and was laid out on a planned grid with imperial palaces at its centre.

kharaj.s: Kharaj was a land tax levied in Islamic states on agricultural land, originally applied to territory conquered by Muslim armies and worked by non-Muslim cultivators. It formed a key source of revenue for the Rashidun and Umayyad Caliphates, where disputes over its payment by…

kharak-singh.s: Kharak Singh was the eldest son and successor of Ranjit Singh, founder of the Sikh Empire. His brief reign after his father's death in 1839 was dominated by court intrigue, and he died under suspicious circumstances in 1840.

kharijites.s: The Kharijites were an early Islamic sectarian movement that broke away from the caliph Ali after he agreed to arbitration with Muawiya at Siffin in 657. They held that leadership should be determined by piety rather than descent and rejected rulers they judged sinful.

khazar-khaganate.s: The Khazar Khaganate was a Turkic steppe state that controlled the region between the Black Sea, the Caspian and the Volga from the seventh to the tenth century. Emerging from the western fringes of the Gokturk world, it grew wealthy from trade between Europe, the Islamic…

khitans.s: The Khitans were a nomadic people of the Mongolian and Manchurian steppe who founded the Liao dynasty in northern China in the tenth century. Earlier they had been among the peoples subject to or neighbouring the Gokturk Empire.

khiva.s: Khiva is a city in the Khwarazm region of present-day Uzbekistan, long the capital of the Khanate of Khiva. Nader Shah of the Afsharid Empire campaigned against it in 1740 during his Central Asian expeditions.

khmelnytsky-uprising.s: The Khmelnytsky Uprising was a Cossack rebellion that began in 1648 under Bohdan Khmelnytsky in the Ukrainian lands of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Drawing on Cossack, peasant and Orthodox grievances against Polish magnates, it inflicted heavy defeats on Commonwealth…

khmer-empire.s: The Khmer Empire was a Hindu-Buddhist state centred on Angkor in present-day Cambodia, dominant in mainland South-East Asia from the ninth to the fifteenth century. It is known for monumental temple complexes such as Angkor Wat and for an elaborate system of reservoirs and…

khorasan.s: Khorasan is a historical region of north-eastern Iran and adjoining parts of Central Asia and Afghanistan, containing cities such as Nishapur, Merv and Herat. It was the launching ground of the Abbasid revolution against the Umayyad Caliphate and the base from which the…

khorsabad.s: Khorsabad is the modern name of the site of Dur-Sharrukin, the royal city built by the Assyrian king Sargon II in northern Iraq in the late eighth century BCE. Its palace was decorated with monumental reliefs and colossal winged bull figures.

khosrow-i.s: Khosrow I, also known as Anushirvan, was a Sasanian king who reigned in the sixth century CE and is remembered as one of the dynasty's greatest rulers. He reformed taxation and the army, strengthening central control over the Sasanian Empire.

khosrow-ii.s: Khosrow II was the last great king of the Sasanian Empire, reigning in the late sixth and early seventh centuries CE. His long war against the Byzantine Empire brought Sasanian armies to Egypt and Anatolia before a Byzantine counter-offensive reversed these gains.

khutba.s: The khutba is the sermon delivered at Friday congregational prayer in Islam, in which the name of the recognised ruler was traditionally proclaimed. Inclusion or omission of a ruler's name in the khutba was therefore a public sign of political allegiance.

khvarenah.s: Khvarenah, known in Middle Persian as xwarrah, is an Iranian concept of divine glory or royal fortune believed to accompany legitimate rulers. In the Sasanian Empire it formed part of the ideology of kingship, signalling that the monarch ruled with divine favour.

khwarazm.s: Khwarazm is a historical region around the lower Amu Darya river and its delta south of the Aral Sea, in present-day Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. An ancient centre of irrigated agriculture and trade, it gave its name to the Khwarazmian Empire, whose shahs built a large state…

khwarazmian-empire.s: The Khwarazmian Empire was a Persianate Muslim state ruled by the Khwarazm Shahs, which grew from the Khwarazm region into a major power in Central Asia and Iran around 1200. It displaced the Seljuks in much of the east.

khwarazmians.s: The Khwarazmians were the people and ruling dynasty of Khwarazm, whose shahs built the Khwarazmian Empire. They rose at the expense of the declining Seljuk Empire in the twelfth century.

khyber-pass.s: The Khyber Pass is a mountain pass linking Afghanistan with the plains of the north-western Indian subcontinent, in present-day Pakistan. It has long been a key route for armies and trade entering India.

kidinuid-dynasty.s: The Kidinuid dynasty was a ruling line of Elam that revived Elamite power around 1500 BCE. According to the Elamite Confederation profile, it introduced the unifying title King of Anshan and Susa, reasserting Elamite cultural identity after periods of Mesopotamian influence.

kiel.s: Kiel is a port city on the Baltic coast of northern Germany and was the principal base of the German Empire's navy. Its harbour and the Kiel Canal gave it strategic importance.

kiel-mutiny.s: The Kiel mutiny was a revolt by sailors of the German High Seas Fleet in 1918, sparked by orders for a final naval sortie against the British at the end of the First World War. The unrest spread rapidly to other cities, giving rise to workers' and soldiers' councils.

kievan-rus.s: Kievan Rus' was a medieval East Slavic state centred on Kyiv, flourishing from the late ninth to the thirteenth century. Its rulers attacked and helped destroy the Khazar Khaganate in the tenth century, removing a major power on the steppe.

kindattu.s: Kindattu was a king of the Shimashki dynasty of Elam. Around 2004 BCE he sacked Ur and captured the last ruler of the Third Dynasty of Ur, ending Mesopotamian hegemony over Elam.

king-of-anshan-and-susa.s: King of Anshan and Susa was a royal title of Elamite rulers, joining the names of the highland centre of Anshan and the lowland city of Susa. In the Sukkalmah period it formed one tier of a tripartite governing hierarchy.

king-of-bohemia.s: The King of Bohemia was the ruler of the Kingdom of Bohemia, a constituent realm of the Holy Roman Empire centred on Prague. Under the Golden Bull of 1356 the King of Bohemia was one of the seven prince-electors who chose the emperor.

king-of-the-lombards.s: King of the Lombards was the title of the rulers of the Lombard kingdom in Italy. After Charlemagne conquered the kingdom in 774, he assumed the title himself, adding Italy to the Frankish realm.

king-of-the-universe.s: King of the Universe, or King of the World, was a prestigious Mesopotamian royal title signifying universal rule. First used by Akkadian kings, it was later adopted by Assyrian rulers to express claims to supremacy over all lands.

kingdom-of-aragon.s: The Kingdom of Aragon was a Christian kingdom in north-eastern Iberia that took part in the Reconquista against the Almoravid and Almohad states of al-Andalus. Through union with Catalonia it built a Mediterranean presence.

kingdom-of-castile.s: The Kingdom of Castile was a Christian kingdom of central Iberia and the leading power of the Reconquista. It fought both the Almoravid Empire and the Almohad Caliphate, notably at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.

kingdom-of-dahomey.s: The Kingdom of Dahomey was a West African kingdom centred on Abomey in present-day Benin, known for its centralised monarchy and its role in the Atlantic slave trade. In the eighteenth century it was forced to pay tribute to the Oyo Empire after repeated Oyo cavalry invasions.

kingdom-of-great-britain.s: The Kingdom of Great Britain was the state created by the union of England and Scotland in 1707. It united the two realms under one parliament at Westminster and combined their commercial and colonial interests.

kingdom-of-hungary.s: The Kingdom of Hungary was a central European kingdom ruled by the Habsburgs from the sixteenth century onwards. Under the Compromise of 1867 it became an equal partner in the Dual Monarchy, governing its half of the state, known as Transleithania, with its own parliament.

kingdom-of-israel.s: The Kingdom of Israel was the northern Israelite kingdom of the Levant, with its capital at Samaria. It was conquered by the Assyrian Empire around 720 BCE, and much of its population was deported in line with Assyrian resettlement policy.

kingdom-of-italy.s: The Kingdom of Italy was the unified Italian state proclaimed in 1861 under the House of Savoy, lasting until the republic was established in 1946. It built the Italian Empire through colonies in Eritrea, Somalia and Libya and the invasion of Ethiopia.

kingdom-of-jerusalem.s: The Kingdom of Jerusalem was a Crusader state established in the Levant after the First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099. Its army was decisively defeated by Saladin, founder of the Ayyubid Empire, at the Battle of Hattin in 1187, after which Jerusalem itself fell.

kingdom-of-kanem.s: The Kingdom of Kanem was a state to the north-east of Lake Chad, ruled by the Sayfawa dynasty, which converted to Islam around the eleventh century. It controlled trans-Saharan trade routes towards North Africa.

kingdom-of-kongo.s: The Kingdom of Kongo was a Central African state centred on Mbanza Kongo in present-day northern Angola, flourishing from the fourteenth century. It entered into contact with Portugal in the 1480s, and its rulers adopted Christianity.

kingdom-of-macedon.s: The Kingdom of Macedon was an ancient Greek kingdom in the northern Balkans. Under Philip II it became the dominant power in Greece, and his son Alexander the Great used it as the base for conquering the Persian Empire.

kingdom-of-navarre.s: The Kingdom of Navarre was a small Christian kingdom in the western Pyrenees of northern Iberia. Its forces joined the Castilian and Aragonese armies that defeated the Almohad Caliphate at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.

kingdom-of-poland.s: The Kingdom of Poland, also known as the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland, was the Polish state that entered a union with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. After a long personal union under the Jagiellonian dynasty, the two were joined by the Union of Lublin in 1569.

kingdom-of-portugal.s: The Kingdom of Portugal was a monarchy on the Atlantic coast of Iberia, formed during the Reconquista against the Almoravid and Almohad states. From the fifteenth century it launched voyages that built the Portuguese Empire across Africa, Asia and Brazil.

kingdom-of-prussia.s: The Kingdom of Prussia was a German state ruled by the Hohenzollern dynasty from 1701, known for its efficient bureaucracy and powerful army. It gained territory from Sweden and in the partitions of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and rivalled Austria within the Holy Roman…

kingdom-of-sine.s: The Kingdom of Sine was a Serer kingdom in present-day Senegal, located in the region dominated by the Jolof Empire. It was among the polities associated with the Jolof confederation in its early period.

kingdom-of-the-lombards.s: The Kingdom of the Lombards was a Germanic kingdom established in Italy after the Lombard invasion of 568. Its pressure on the papacy led popes to seek Frankish protection, and Charlemagne conquered the kingdom in 774.

kingdom-of-the-netherlands.s: The Kingdom of the Netherlands is the Dutch monarchy established in 1815 after the Napoleonic Wars, succeeding the Dutch Republic. It governed the later phase of the Dutch Empire, including the Dutch East Indies, until decolonisation after the Second World War.

kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia.s: The Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia was a state built by the Amorite ruler Shamshi-Adad I in northern Mesopotamia in the early second millennium BCE. It brought Ashur and other northern cities under one rule and is often treated as a precursor of Assyrian power.

kingdom-of-zimbabwe.s: The Kingdom of Zimbabwe was the state centred on Great Zimbabwe on the Zimbabwe plateau, which flourished from about the twelfth to the fifteenth century. Its stone enclosures and gold trade with the Swahili coast made it a major southern African power.

kish.s: Kish was an ancient Sumerian city in central Mesopotamia, associated in tradition with the first kingship after the flood. Sargon of Akkad rose to power from service at Kish before founding the Akkadian Empire.

kitab-al-farq.s: Kitab al-Farq, or Book of the Difference, is a political treatise by Usman dan Fodio, founder of the Sokoto Caliphate. It contrasts just Islamic government with the practices of the Hausa rulers he opposed.

kitbuqa.s: Kitbuqa was a Mongol general of Naiman origin who served under Hulagu, founder of the Ilkhanate. He commanded the Mongol forces left in Syria after Hulagu withdrew, and was defeated and killed by the Mamluks at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260.

knighthood.s: Knighthood refers to the tradition of an elite class of mounted, heavily armed warriors bound by status and service to a ruler. Its armoured cavalry influenced Byzantine heavy cavalry and, through several channels of transmission, the medieval European knightly tradition.

kobbei.s: Kobbei was a commercial town in northern Darfur and an early capital or chief trading centre of the Darfur Sultanate. It stood at the southern end of the Darb el-Arba'in, the trans-Saharan caravan route linking Darfur to Asyut in Egypt.

koh-i-noor.s: The Koh-i-Noor, meaning 'Mountain of Light', is one of the most famous diamonds in the world, originating in India. Nader Shah of the Afsharid Empire carried it off from Delhi along with the Peacock Throne after his invasion of Mughal India in 1739.

koine-greek.s: Koine Greek was the common form of Greek that spread across the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East after the conquests of Alexander the Great. It served as the language of administration, commerce and culture in the Hellenistic kingdoms, including the Seleucid Empire.

kokand.s: Kokand is a city in the Fergana Valley of present-day Uzbekistan and was the capital of the Khanate of Kokand from the eighteenth century. The khanate was one of the Central Asian states conquered by the Russian Empire in the nineteenth century.

kola-nut.s: The kola nut is the caffeine-containing seed of the kola tree, native to the West African forest zone. It was chewed as a stimulant, used in social and ceremonial exchange, and widely traded northwards into the savannah and Sahel.

komnenian-dynasty.s: The Komnenian dynasty ruled the Byzantine Empire from 1081 to 1185, beginning with Alexios I Komnenos. Its emperors restored Byzantine military and political strength after the crises of the eleventh century, partly by relying on family networks and Western mercenaries.

konkan-coast.s: The Konkan coast is the strip of land along the western coast of India between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea. It was strategically important to the Maratha Empire, which built coastal forts and a navy there.

kontagora.s: Kontagora was an emirate and town in present-day north-western Nigeria, part of the Sokoto Caliphate. It was among the first emirates conquered by British forces under Frederick Lugard, falling in 1900.

konya.s: Konya is a city in central Anatolia, the ancient Iconium. It became the capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, the Anatolian branch of the Seljuk world, and flourished as a centre of trade, architecture and learning.

kopek.s: The kopek is a small unit of Russian currency, one hundredth of a rouble. Its name is usually traced to the spear (kopyo) carried by the mounted figure on Muscovite coins introduced in the 1530s.

kopje.s: A kopje is a small, isolated hill, often a rocky granite outcrop, rising from the surrounding plain in southern Africa. Such features are characteristic of the Zimbabwe plateau.

kora.s: The kora is a twenty-one-string harp-lute of the Mandinka and neighbouring peoples of West Africa, played above all by jali (griots), the hereditary musicians and keepers of oral history. Mandinka tradition places its origin in the Kaabu Empire, whose rulers and wars are…

kordofan.s: Kordofan is a region of present-day Sudan lying between Darfur and the Nile valley. It was a contested borderland over which the Darfur Sultanate and its eastern neighbours fought for control of trade and resources.

korea.s: Korea is the peninsula in north-east Asia between China and Japan, home to a succession of Korean kingdoms. It was deeply connected to Chinese dynasties, with the Han Dynasty establishing commanderies there, the Tang Dynasty intervening in its wars, and the Ming Empire…

kosciuszko-uprising.s: The Kosciuszko Uprising was a revolt led by Tadeusz Kosciuszko in 1794 against Russian and Prussian domination of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth following the Second Partition. Despite early successes, it was crushed by Russian and Prussian forces.

kosmoi.s: The kosmoi were the chief magistrates of the city-states of ancient Crete. Aristotle compared the constitution of Carthage with those of Sparta and Crete, drawing an analogy between Carthaginian institutions and the Spartan ephors and Cretan kosmoi.

kotoko-council.s: The Kotoko Council was the governing council of the Ashanti Empire, established at the empire's foundation around 1700. It brought together the paramount chiefs of the constituent Asante states, and its collective assent was required for major decisions such as war, treaties…

koumbi-saleh.s: Koumbi Saleh is an archaeological site in south-eastern Mauritania widely identified as the capital of the Ghana Empire. Arabic sources describe a twin city with a Muslim merchant quarter and a royal town.

kouroukan-fouga.s: The Kouroukan Fouga is the founding charter traditionally attributed to the assembly convened by Sundiata Keita after the creation of the Mali Empire in the thirteenth century. Preserved in oral tradition, it set out rules for the empire's social organisation, clan relations…

koutoubia-mosque.s: The Koutoubia Mosque is the principal mosque of Marrakesh, built under the Almohad Caliphate in the twelfth century. Its minaret is one of the finest examples of Almohad architecture and influenced later towers such as the Giralda of Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat.

koxinga.s: Koxinga, born Zheng Chenggong, was a seventeenth-century Ming loyalist commander who resisted the Qing conquest of China from bases on the south-eastern coast. In 1662 he expelled the Dutch East India Company from Taiwan after besieging Fort Zeelandia.

kubar.s: Kubar was a later capital of the Aksumite kingdom, to which the court relocated in the ninth century as Aksum declined. Its precise location remains uncertain.

kublai-khan.s: Kublai Khan was a grandson of Genghis Khan who became Great Khan of the Mongol Empire and founded the Yuan Dynasty in China. He completed the conquest of the Song Dynasty in 1279 and ruled from Khanbaliq.

kufa.s: Kufa was a garrison city founded by Arab Muslim forces in southern Iraq in the 630s during the Rashidun conquests. It became a major political and religious centre and served as the capital of the caliph Ali.

kul-tigin.s: Kul Tigin was a prince and military commander of the Second Turkic Khaganate, brother of the ruler Bilge Khagan. He died in 731, and his memorial inscription in the Orkhon valley is one of the earliest surviving texts in the Old Turkic language.

kulturkampf.s: The Kulturkampf was a political conflict in the 1870s between the government of Otto von Bismarck and the Catholic Church in the newly founded German Empire. Laws restricted the Church's role in education and appointments, reflecting suspicion of Catholic loyalties.

kumaradevi.s: Kumaradevi was a Licchavi princess who married Chandragupta I, regarded as the true founder of the Gupta Empire. The marriage brought the Guptas territory and prestige through alliance with the long-established Licchavi clan.

kumasi.s: Kumasi is a city in present-day Ghana and was the capital of the Ashanti Empire. It was the seat of the Asantehene and the Golden Stool, and the centre of the empire's government and trade.

kumwimbe-ngombe.s: Kumwimbe Ngombe was a ruler of the Luba Empire in Central Africa, whose reign is dated to about 1810 to 1840. He is counted among the kings of the empire's apogee, between Ilunga Sungu and Ilunga Kabale.

kumwimbe-tshimbu.s: Kumwimbe Tshimbu was a claimant to the Luba throne in the late nineteenth century. After the death of Ilunga Kabale, he fought a civil war against his rival Kasongo Nyembo.

kupechestvo.s: Kupechestvo was the merchant estate of the Russian Empire, the legally defined class of urban traders. Merchants were organised into guilds according to their declared capital and held particular rights and obligations.

kurdistan.s: Kurdistan is a mountainous region inhabited largely by Kurds, spanning parts of present-day Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Syria. It formed a frontier zone between the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire, and its control was repeatedly contested in their wars.

kurds.s: The Kurds are an Iranian-speaking people of the mountainous region of Kurdistan in the Middle East. The Ayyubid dynasty was of Kurdish origin, and Saladin, its founder, rose to power through service in Zengid armies.

kurgan.s: A kurgan is a burial mound raised over a grave, a form of tomb common across the Eurasian steppe from prehistoric times. Elite Xiongnu burials were placed in such mounds, and their contents, including Chinese bronzes, Bactrian gold work and Roman glassware, reveal the wide…

kurultai.s: A kurultai was a political and military assembly of Mongol and Turkic chiefs, convened to choose leaders and decide major matters. At the kurultai of 1206, Temujin was proclaimed Genghis Khan, marking the foundation of the Mongol Empire.

kuruva.s: Kuruva was a system of tribute and taxation used in the Zimbabwe plateau states. According to the Rozvi Empire's profile, the Rozvi inherited it from the Mutapa, requiring traders operating within the empire to pay tribute directly to the Changamire's court.

kushan-empire.s: The Kushan Empire was a state founded by the Yuezhi in Bactria that expanded into northern India in the first centuries CE. Its control of trade routes between China, India, Persia and the Roman world made it wealthy, and it patronised Buddhism and Gandharan art.

kushite-empire.s: The Kushite Empire, or Kingdom of Kush, was a Nubian state on the middle Nile in present-day Sudan, centred successively on Kerma, Napata and Meroe. Long under Egyptian New Kingdom rule, Kush later conquered Egypt and ruled it as the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty in the eighth and…

kutama-berbers.s: The Kutama were a Berber tribal confederation of the mountains of eastern Algeria. Converted by the Ismaili missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shii, they provided the military force that overthrew the Aghlabids and established the Fatimid Caliphate in 909.

kutik-inshushinak.s: Kutik-Inshushinak (also read Puzur-Inshushinak) was the last king of the Awan dynasty of Elam, ruling around 2100 BCE. After the collapse of Akkadian power he freed Susa, brought Anshan and much of the Iranian plateau under his rule and campaigned into northern Babylonia,…

kutir-nahhunte.s: Kutir-Nahhunte was a king of the Shutrukid dynasty of Elam, the son of Shutruk-Nahhunte. Around 1158 BCE father and son defeated the Kassite dynasty of Babylon, carrying off monuments such as the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin and the Code of Hammurabi to Susa.

kwame-nkrumah.s: Kwame Nkrumah was the leader of the Gold Coast's independence movement and the first prime minister and president of Ghana, which became independent in 1957. He chose the name Ghana in tribute to the medieval Ghana Empire, though the old empire lay far to the north-west.

kwantung-army.s: The Kwantung Army was a group of the Imperial Japanese Army stationed in north-east China from the early twentieth century. Its officers staged the Mukden Incident of 1931, which led to the occupation of Manchuria, and often acted independently of the government in Tokyo.

kyoto.s: Kyoto is a city in central Japan that served as the imperial capital for over a thousand years. During the Tokugawa Shogunate the emperor and court remained in Kyoto, while real political power lay with the shogun in Edo.

karl-theodor-von-dalberg.s: Karl Theodor von Dalberg was the last Elector and Archbishop of Mainz and Archchancellor of the Holy Roman Empire. He allied with Napoleon, kept a state based on Aschaffenburg and Regensburg after the secularisations of 1803, and became Prince-Primate of the Confederation of…

knights-hospitaller.s: The Knights Hospitaller, the Order of Saint John, grew from a hospital for pilgrims in Jerusalem into a military order of the crusades. After the fall of Acre they ruled Rhodes from 1310 to 1522 and Malta from 1530 to 1798, fighting the Ottomans at sea.

kathiawar-agency.s: The Kathiawar Agency was the British political agency, based at Rajkot, that supervised the more than two hundred princely states and chiefships of the Kathiawar peninsula in Gujarat, from great states such as Junagadh and Bhavnagar to tiny talukas. It settled disputes and…

kathmandu-valley.s: The Kathmandu Valley is a fertile basin in the hills of central Nepal containing the cities of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur. It was the heart of the Licchavi kingdom from the 5th century and of the Malla kings, whose realm split into three city kingdoms in the 15th century,…

khmer-rouge.s: The Khmer Rouge was the name given to the Communist Party of Kampuchea and its armed forces. Led by Pol Pot, it fought the Khmer Republic, took Phnom Penh in April 1975 and ruled as Democratic Kampuchea, emptying the cities and causing the deaths of around 1.5 to 2 million…

khama-iii.s: Khama III was kgosi of the Bangwato in present-day Botswana from 1875 to 1923. A Christian convert, he banned alcohol, reformed customs and moved his capital to Palapye and later Serowe.

kim-il-sung.s: Kim Il Sung was a Korean communist who fought as a guerrilla against Japan in Manchuria and later served in the Soviet army. Brought back to Korea by the Soviet occupation in 1945, he became chairman of the Provisional People's Committee for North Korea in 1946 and leader of…

king-wu-of-zhou.s: King Wu was the founding king of the Zhou dynasty. Continuing the work of his father King Wen, he led the Zhou and their allies against the Shang and defeated its last king, Di Xin, at the Battle of Muye, traditionally dated 1046 BCE.

kadi-burhan-al-din.s: Kadi Burhan al-Din was a jurist and poet from Kayseri who served the Eretnid dynasty as judge and vizier. In 1381 he took the throne himself, ruling central Anatolia from Sivas.

karl-renner.s: Karl Renner was an Austrian Social Democratic politician who led the government of German-Austria as state chancellor from 1918 to 1920. In April 1945, as the Red Army took Vienna, he formed a provisional government that declared Austria's independence from Germany.

kuala-lumpur.s: Kuala Lumpur grew from a tin-mining settlement founded around 1857 at the meeting of the Klang and Gombak rivers in Selangor. Chinese miners and their leaders such as Yap Ah Loy built it up, and in 1880 it became the capital of Selangor.

kvirike-iii-of-kakheti.s: Kvirike III, called the Great, was the ruler of Kakheti in eastern Georgia who took the title king around 1010, creating the Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti. He defended its independence against the united Georgian monarchy of Bagrat III and his successors.

karamanoglu-mehmed-bey.s: Karamanoğlu Mehmed Bey was the son of Karaman Bey, founder of the Karamanid beylik in the Taurus mountains. In 1277 he occupied Konya, capital of the declining Sultanate of Rum, and is reported to have decreed that Turkish alone be used at court and in government.

kapilendra-deva.s: Kapilendra Deva was a minister and general of the last Eastern Ganga king who seized the throne of Odisha in 1434 and founded the Suryavamsi Gajapati dynasty. A devotee of Jagannath at Puri, he fought the Bahmani Sultanate, Vijayanagara and the Bengal Sultanate, and his armies…

king-tom-koya.s: King Tom was a Temne subchief of the Koya kingdom who ruled villages on the Sierra Leone peninsula under King Naimbana in the 1780s. In 1787 he agreed to let British abolitionists settle land on the peninsula for the Province of Freedom, a grant that Naimbana confirmed in 1788.

king-wu-of-chu.s: King Wu of Chu, personal name Xiong Tong, ruled the State of Chu from 740 to 690 BCE. In 704 BCE he became the first ruler of Chu to take the title of king, rejecting the Zhou order in which only the Zhou ruler was king.

konstantin-pats.s: Konstantin Päts was an Estonian journalist and politician who headed the Provincial Government of 1917 and the provisional government of the new Republic of Estonia in 1918, during the War of Independence. He served several times as State Elder, and in 1934 he and General…

koca-sinan-pasha.s: Koca Sinan Pasha was an Ottoman general and statesman of Albanian origin. He reconquered Yemen from the Zaydi rebels in 1569 to 1571 and in 1574 took Tunis and La Goulette from Spain, ending the Hafsid dynasty.

kunta-kinteh-island.s: Kunta Kinteh Island is a small island in the Gambia River, formerly St Andrew's Island and then James Island. Courland built a fort there in 1651; the Dutch seized it in 1659 and the English in 1661, naming it after the Duke of York.

kahekili-ii.s: Kahekili II was the ruling chief of Maui from about 1765. In 1783 he conquered Oʻahu, and with his half-brother Kaʻeokulani of Kauaʻi he came to dominate most of the Hawaiian Islands apart from Hawaiʻi itself.

kahk-tiliw-chan-chaak.s: K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Chaak was a king of the Classic Maya city of Naranjo, enthroned in 693 as a child, with his mother Lady Six Sky of Dos Pilas acting as ruler. He fought a series of wars against neighbouring cities such as Ucanal and Yaxha, and in 710 claimed a victory over…

kaji-imox.s: Kaji' Imox was one of the two kings of the Kaqchikel Maya at Iximche in highland Guatemala. With Beleheb' Kat he welcomed Pedro de Alvarado in 1524 and allied with the Spanish against the K'iche'.

kalonga-masula.s: Kalonga Masula was a ruler of the Maravi confederacy, in what is now Malawi, in the early 17th century. He extended Maravi power towards the Indian Ocean coast and brought the Lundu kingdom back under Maravi overlordship, and aided the Portuguese against the Zimba.

kapaya-nayaka.s: Kapaya Nayaka of the Musunuri family was a former Kakatiya commander who, allied with the founders of the Vijayanagara Empire, recaptured Warangal from the Tughluq governor around 1336. He ruled Telangana from Warangal and supported the rebellion that founded the Bahmani…

kara-mahmud-pasha-bushati.s: Kara Mahmud Pasha Bushati was the hereditary Ottoman pasha of Scutari (Shkodër) in northern Albania from 1775. He expanded his domain, negotiated directly with Austria and repeatedly defied the Ottoman government.

karaeng-matoaya.s: Karaeng Matoaya was ruler of Tallo and chancellor of the twin Makassar kingdom of Gowa. In 1605 he became the first Makassar ruler to accept Islam, together with Sultan Alauddin of Gowa, and he guided the wars that forced Islam on the Bugis states.

karamokho-alfa.s: Karamokho Alfa, Ibrahima Sambegu, was a Fulbe Muslim scholar who around 1725 led a jihad in the Futa Jallon highlands of present-day Guinea against the Jallonke rulers. He became the first almamy of the Imamate of Futa Jallon, a theocratic state that inspired later West…

karl-thopia.s: Karl Thopia was an Albanian nobleman who held lands in central Albania between the Mat and Shkumbin rivers in the 14th century. Claiming Angevin descent through his mother, he seized Durrës from the Angevins in 1368 and styled himself Prince of Albania.

karlis-ulmanis.s: Kārlis Ulmanis was a Latvian statesman who became the first prime minister of the Republic of Latvia when it was proclaimed in November 1918. His government fought the Latvian Socialist Soviet Republic, German forces and the Bermontians in the War of Independence.

ken-arok.s: Ken Arok was the founder of the Singhasari kingdom in eastern Java. According to Javanese chronicles he rose from humble origins to rule Tumapel, and in 1222 he defeated Kertajaya, the last king of Kediri, at the Battle of Ganter.

kennedy-simmonds.s: Kennedy Simmonds is a Kittitian politician who was the first prime minister of Saint Kitts and Nevis. Leader of the People's Action Movement, he became premier of the associated state in 1980 and led the islands to independence from Britain on 19 September 1983.

kenneth-macalpin.s: Kenneth MacAlpin was a king of Gaelic origin who became ruler of the Picts around 843. Later tradition made him the founder of the Kingdom of Scotland, uniting the Picts with the Gaels of Dál Riata, although the merger into the kingdom of Alba took several more generations.

khoja-niyaz.s: Khoja Niyaz was a Uyghur leader from Kumul (Hami) who headed the Kumul rebellion against the Xinjiang provincial government from 1931. In 1933 he was named president of the First East Turkestan Republic at Kashgar, although he never governed from there.

ki-ageng-pemanahan.s: Ki Ageng Pemanahan was a Javanese noble who served Hadiwijaya of Pajang and helped him defeat Arya Penangsang in the succession war after Trenggana's death. As a reward he received the land of Mataram, where he founded a settlement at Kotagede.

kilij-arslan-i.s: Kilij Arslan I was sultan of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum from 1092 to 1107. He destroyed the People's Crusade in 1096 but lost his capital Nicaea to the First Crusade in 1097 and was defeated at Dorylaeum.

kilij-arslan-ii.s: Kilij Arslan II was sultan of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum from 1156 to 1192. He annexed the lands of the Danishmendids in the 1170s and destroyed a Byzantine army under Manuel I Komnenos at Myriokephalon in 1176, ending Byzantine hopes of recovering central Anatolia.

king-cheng-of-zhou.s: King Cheng of Zhou was the second king of the Western Zhou, son of King Wu. Because he came to the throne young, his uncle the Duke of Zhou ruled as regent, crushing a major rebellion and consolidating Zhou rule in the east.

king-nan-of-zhou.s: King Nan of Zhou was the last king of the Zhou dynasty, reigning from 314 to 256 BCE. By his time royal power was nominal, and he lived under the protection of the Duchy of Western Zhou.

king-ping-of-zhou.s: King Ping of Zhou was the first king of the Eastern Zhou, reigning from 770 to 720 BCE. After the Quanrong sacked Haojing and killed his father King You in 771 BCE, he moved the court east to Luoyi (Luoyang) with the support of Jin, Zheng and Qin.

king-philips-war.s: King Philip's War was fought in 1675–1676 between English colonists in New England and Native peoples led by the Wampanoag sachem Metacom, known to the English as King Philip. It was one of the deadliest wars of colonial American history and devastated Plymouth Colony and…

king-wen-of-zhou.s: King Wen of Zhou was the leader of the Zhou people in the Wei River valley in the late Shang period. He built up Zhou power and alliances, and his son King Wu went on to overthrow the Shang around 1046 BCE.

king-wen-of-chu.s: King Wen of Chu ruled the State of Chu from 689 to 677 BCE. A son of King Wu of Chu and Deng Man, a princess of Deng, he moved the Chu capital to Ying and extended Chu power north of the Han River.

kinich-yax-kuk-mo.s: K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' was the founder of the royal dynasty of Copán, in present-day Honduras, who took power in 426 CE. Inscriptions link him to Teotihuacan and Tikal, and a tomb believed to be his lies deep beneath the Acropolis.

kizhavan-sethupathi.s: Kizhavan Sethupathi, also called Raghunatha Kilavan, ruled the Ramnad kingdom on the south-eastern coast of Tamil Nadu from about 1671 to 1710. He threw off the overlordship of the Madurai Nayaks and made the Sethupathis independent rulers.

krishnaraja-wodeyar-iii.s: Krishnaraja Wodeyar III was maharaja of Mysore from 1799 to 1868. After Tipu Sultan's defeat in 1799 the British placed him on the throne as a five-year-old, with the diwan Purnaiah governing.

kubja-vishnuvardhana.s: Kubja Vishnuvardhana was the founder of the Eastern Chalukya dynasty of Vengi in coastal Andhra. A younger brother of Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas of Badami, he was made viceroy of the Vengi region after its conquest from the Vishnukundina dynasty around 624.

kuchuk-muhammad.s: Küchük Muhammad was a khan of the Golden Horde in the mid 15th century, ruling from Sarai as the Horde broke apart. His rump state, known as the Great Horde, claimed seniority among the Jochid successor states.

kujula-kadphises.s: Kujula Kadphises was the founder of the Kushan Empire in the 1st century CE. Chief of the Kushan branch of the Yuezhi in Bactria, he united the five Yuezhi chiefdoms and extended his rule south across the Hindu Kush into Gandhara.

kurt-eisner.s: Kurt Eisner was a German journalist and Independent Social Democrat who led the revolution in Munich on 7 November 1918, proclaiming Bavaria a republic and ending Wittelsbach rule. He became the first premier of the Free State of Bavaria.

king-xuan-of-zhou.s: King Xuan of Zhou was the eleventh king of the Western Zhou dynasty, who came to the throne after the Gonghe regency. He restored royal authority, campaigning against the Xianyun in the north and the Huai peoples in the south.

kerch-strait.s: The Kerch Strait, the Cimmerian Bosporus of the ancient Greeks, links the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov between Crimea and the Taman peninsula. From the 6th century BCE Greek colonies such as Panticapaeum and Phanagoria lined its shores, and around 480 BCE they united as the…

kaew-nawarat.s: Kaew Nawarat was the last ruler of Chiang Mai, a descendant of Kawila, reigning from 1911 to 1939 under Siamese authority. By his time Lan Na had been absorbed into Siam's provincial system, and his role was largely ceremonial.

kaibil-balam.s: Kaibil Balam was the ruler of the Mam Maya kingdom in the western highlands of Guatemala at the time of the Spanish conquest. In 1525 Gonzalo de Alvarado besieged his fortified capital of Zaculeu for several months, and Kaibil Balam surrendered when his people were starving,…

kak-tiliw-chan-yopaat.s: K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat was the ruler of the Maya city of Quiriguá, installed in 724 under the authority of Copán. In 738 he captured and sacrificed Copán's king Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil, freeing Quiriguá and taking control of trade on the Motagua river.

kalbali-khan.s: Kalbali Khan was a khan of Nakhichevan of the Kangarlu tribe in the late eighteenth century. He resisted Agha Muhammad Khan Qajar's efforts to reassert Iranian control over the South Caucasus khanates, and the Qajar ruler had him blinded.

kalyan-chand.s: Kalyan Chand was a raja of the Chand dynasty of Kumaon in the central Himalaya. Around 1563 he moved the capital from Champawat to Almora, which remained the centre of the kingdom until the Gorkha conquest of 1790 and is still the main town of the region.

kamachat-aslamie.s: Kamachat Aslamie was the paramount chief of the Middag chiefdom of Taiwan's west-central plains, known from Dutch East India Company records as the King of Middag. He presided over a confederation of some fifteen to twenty-seven villages of the Papora, Babuza and related…

kamehameha-i.s: Kamehameha I was a chief of Hawaiʻi Island who conquered Maui, Molokaʻi and Oʻahu in a series of campaigns, winning the decisive Battle of Nuʻuanu in 1795. He founded the Kingdom of Hawaii, and Kauaʻi accepted his rule in 1810.

kamehameha-iii.s: Kamehameha III was king of Hawaii from 1825 to 1854, the longest reign of the monarchy. He issued the kingdom's first constitution in 1840 and the Great Māhele of 1848, which introduced private land ownership and allowed foreigners to buy land.

kameshwar-thakur.s: Kameshwar Thakur was a Maithil Brahmin of the Oinwar family who received Mithila from the Tughluq rulers of the Delhi Sultanate after they overthrew the Karnat dynasty in 1324. Governing on their behalf, he founded the Oinwar dynasty, whose later kings, notably Shivasimha,…

kamil-pasha-al-qudsi.s: Kamil Pasha al-Qudsi was an Aleppine notable who served as the first governor of the State of Aleppo, created by the French Mandate authorities in 1920. He governed under French supervision as the city's merchants suffered from new borders cutting Aleppo off from Anatolia.

kamran-shah-durrani.s: Kamran Shah Durrani was a Sadozai prince, son of Mahmud Shah Durrani. When the Barakzai brothers took over most of the Durrani Empire around 1818, he and his father held on to Herat as an independent principality.

kan-bozhou.s: Kan Bozhou was a Chinese noble whom the Rouran Khaganate installed as king of Gaochang in the Turfan oasis in 460, after destroying the Northern Liang remnant there. His was the first of several short-lived dynasties of the Gaochang Kingdom before the Qu family took the throne…

kan-ii.s: K'an II was king of the Maya city of Caracol in Belize from 618 to 658. Allied with the Kaan dynasty of Calakmul, he waged war against Naranjo and defeated it in 631.

kan-joy-chitam-ii.s: K'an Joy Chitam II was king of the Maya city of Palenque from 702, a son of K'inich Janaab' Pakal. In 711 he was captured by the rival city of Toniná, which depicted him bound as a prisoner on a relief.

kan-maax.s: Kan Maax was the last known king of the Maya city of Cancuén in Guatemala, son of Taj Chan Ahk. Around 800 he, his queen and about thirty nobles were killed and their bodies placed in a palace cistern, after which the city was abandoned.

kangshu-feng.s: Kangshu Feng was a younger brother of King Wu of Zhou. After the Rebellion of the Three Guards, the Duke of Zhou granted him the former Shang capital region around Zhaoge in northern Henan to watch over the conquered Shang population.

karadorde.s: Karađorđe was a livestock trader and former Austrian volunteer whom an assembly at Orašac chose in February 1804 to lead the First Serbian Uprising against the Ottoman janissaries. He won major victories and ruled revolutionary Serbia as supreme leader until the Ottomans…

karakalpak-autonomous-oblast.s: The Karakalpak Autonomous Oblast was a Soviet territory created in 1925 in the Amu Darya delta for the Karakalpaks, from lands of the former Khorezm People's Soviet Republic. It was first attached to the Kazakh ASSR.

karelian-assr.s: The Karelian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was an autonomous republic of the Russian SFSR with its capital at Petrozavodsk. In 1940, after the Winter War, it was combined with territory ceded by Finland to form the Karelo-Finnish SSR, a full union republic.

karesi-bey.s: Karesi Bey was a Turkmen leader who around the end of the thirteenth century took the Byzantine region of Mysia, with Balıkesir and Pergamon, founding the beylik of Karesi. After his death his sons Demirhan and Yakhshi divided the lands and quarrelled, and the Ottomans annexed…

karibil-watar.s: Karib'il Watar was a mukarrib, or ruler, of the kingdom of Saba in south-western Arabia. His great inscription at Sirwah records campaigns that destroyed the kingdom of Awsan, killing thousands, and imposed Sabaean supremacy over much of Yemen.

karka-ii.s: Karka II was the last ruling emperor of the Rashtrakuta dynasty of the Deccan. He came to the throne after the Paramara king Siyaka sacked the capital Manyakheta in 972.

karl-i-prince-of-liechtenstein.s: Karl I, Prince of Liechtenstein, was a Moravian noble who converted to Catholicism and served the Habsburgs, becoming the first prince of his house in 1608. After the Bohemian revolt he was a leading agent of Habsburg repression in Bohemia, and in 1622 Ferdinand II granted him…

karma-kagyu.s: Karma Kagyu is a major school of Tibetan Buddhism, a branch of the Kagyu tradition founded in the twelfth century by the first Karmapa, Düsum Khyenpa. Its Karmapa lamas began the Tibetan practice of recognised reincarnation.

karma-phuntsok-namgyal.s: Karma Phuntsok Namgyal was a king of the Tsangpa dynasty, ruling from Samdrubtse (Shigatse). In 1618 he conquered Ü, ending the last influence of the Phagmodrupa dynasty and bringing most of central Tibet under Tsangpa rule.

karma-tenkyong-wangpo.s: Karma Tenkyong Wangpo was the last king of the Tsangpa dynasty of Tibet, succeeding his father Karma Phuntsok Namgyal around 1620. He opposed the Gelug school, whose allies, the Khoshut Mongols under Güshi Khan, invaded and took his fortress of Samdrubtse in 1642.

karo-batak.s: The Karo Batak are a Batak people of the highlands of North Sumatra in Indonesia, around the Karo plateau above Medan. Linked to the coast by trade in forest products, they were connected with the Aru kingdom and later with the Deli Sultanate, which claimed authority over…

kashu-chaidya.s: Kashu Chaidya was a king of the Chedi people mentioned in the Rigveda, where a hymn praises him for generous gifts of cattle and camels to priests. He is the earliest named ruler of the Chedis, who lived south of the Yamuna in the region of Bundelkhand and later formed one of…

kassym-jomart-tokayev.s: Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is a Kazakh diplomat and politician, formerly foreign minister, prime minister and Director-General of the UN Office at Geneva. He became president of Kazakhstan in 2019 when Nursultan Nazarbayev resigned.

kato-kiyomasa.s: Katō Kiyomasa was a Japanese general of Toyotomi Hideyoshi who received northern Higo in 1588 and became a leading commander in the invasions of Korea. Siding with Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara in 1600, he gained all of Higo and built the great castle of Kumamoto.

kawai-tsugunosuke.s: Kawai Tsugunosuke was a senior retainer of the Nagaoka domain in Echigo who reformed its finances and modernised its army with rifles and Gatling guns. In the Boshin War of 1868 he sought armed neutrality, but when imperial forces refused, he led Nagaoka in one of the…

kawila.s: Kawila was a prince of Lampang who in the 1770s allied with the Thonburi Kingdom of Siam and helped drive the Burmese out of Lan Na. He rebuilt the depopulated city of Chiang Mai from 1796, bringing in war captives as settlers, and ruled it as a Siamese vassal.

kawo-tona-gaga.s: Kawo Tona Gaga was the last independent king of Wolaita in southern Ethiopia. When Emperor Menelik II invaded with a large army in 1894, he led fierce resistance but was wounded and captured.

kaysone-phomvihane.s: Kaysone Phomvihane was the leader of the Lao People's Revolutionary Party and of the communist Pathet Lao movement. When the Lao People's Democratic Republic was proclaimed in December 1975 he became prime minister, holding the post until 1991, and then president until his death.

kazys-grinius.s: Kazys Grinius was a Lithuanian physician and politician of the Peasant Populist Union who served as the third President of Lithuania in 1926. Elected after the left-wing parties won that year's parliamentary election, he was removed within months by the military coup of…

keate-award.s: The Keate Award was the 1871 arbitration by Robert Keate, Lieutenant-Governor of Natal, of rival claims to the land around the newly found diamond fields of southern Africa. It upheld the claims of the Griqua leader Nicolaas Waterboer and of Tswana chiefs against the South…

keith-mitchell.s: Keith Mitchell is a Grenadian politician and former mathematics lecturer who led the New National Party and was Prime Minister of Grenada from 1995 to 2008 and again from 2013 to 2022, the longest tenure in the country's history. His governments faced the destruction caused by…

keladi-chennamma.s: Keladi Chennamma was queen of the Keladi Nayaka kingdom in coastal Karnataka, ruling from 1671 until her death in 1696 after the death of her husband Somashekhara Nayaka. She defended the kingdom against neighbouring powers and, around 1689, gave refuge to Rajaram, son of…

keleshbey-chachba.s: Keleshbey Chachba, also called Kelesh Ahmed-Bey Shervashidze, was prince of Abkhazia in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. A Muslim ruler under Ottoman overlordship, he built up princely power, controlled the port of Sukhum and dealt with both the Ottomans and Russia.

kemal-al-din-husayn-bey.s: Kemal al-Din Husayn Bey was the last important ruler of the Hamidid beylik of south-western Anatolia, centred on Eğirdir. Unable to resist the rising Ottoman state, he sold several of his towns, including Beyşehir and Akşehir, to Sultan Murad I in 1374.

kenny-anthony.s: Kenny Anthony is a Saint Lucian lawyer and politician who led the Saint Lucia Labour Party and served as Prime Minister of Saint Lucia from 1997 to 2006 and again from 2011 to 2016. His first government came to power as the island's banana industry collapsed with the loss of…

keshav-das-of-sitamau.s: Keshav Das was a Rathore Rajput of the ruling family of Ratlam who founded the princely state of Sitamau in Malwa in 1701. His descendants ruled the small state as Rajas under Maratha and then British paramountcy until it joined independent India.

keshin-dalbhya.s: Keshin Dalbhya was a king of the Panchalas named in late Vedic texts, especially the Brahmanas, where he appears as a patron of sacrifice and ritual learning. He is associated with the Keshin clan and with debates over the correct performance of rites.

kesho-das-of-jhabua.s: Kesho Das was a Rathore Rajput who founded the state of Jhabua in western Malwa around 1584. According to the state's tradition, he received the title of Raja from the Mughal court after suppressing Bhil chiefs who had attacked imperial officials, and took Jhabua from its…

khabul-khan.s: Khabul Khan was a Mongol chief of the Borjigin clan who united Mongol clans of the Onon and Kherlen valleys in the early 12th century and is regarded as the first khan of the Khamag Mongol confederation. The Secret History of the Mongols and Chinese sources record his defiance…

khalaf-ibn-ahmad.s: Khalaf ibn Ahmad was the last important Saffarid ruler of Sistan, governing from 963 as an autonomous amir under Samanid and later Ghaznavid pressure. He was known as a patron of scholars and religious learning.

khalifa-bin-hamad-al-thani.s: Khalifa bin Hamad Al Thani was Emir of Qatar from 1972 to 1995. Already the leading figure in government at independence in 1971, he deposed his cousin Ahmad bin Ali in February 1972.

khalkha-mongols.s: The Khalkha Mongols are the largest subgroup of the Mongols and form the majority of the population of present-day Mongolia. Organised by the descendants of Dayan Khan's son Geresenje, they were divided from the 16th century into the Tüsheet, Zasagt and Setsen khanates.

khammao-vilay.s: Khammao Vilay was a Lao official who served as prime minister of the Lao Issara government formed in Vientiane in October 1945 after the Japanese surrender. His cabinet, which included Souvanna Phouma and Souphanouvong, opposed the return of French rule but had little money or…

khan-ahmad-khan.s: Khan Ahmad Khan was the last ruler of the Karkiya dynasty of Lahijan in eastern Gilan, on the Caspian coast of Iran. Long held prisoner by Shah Tahmasp I, he was restored and later quarrelled with Shah Abbas I over marriage alliances and his dealings with the Ottomans.

khana-ratsadon.s: The Khana Ratsadon, or People's Party, was a group of civilian and military officials founded by Thai students in Paris in 1927. Led by Pridi Banomyong and Plaek Phibunsongkhram, it carried out the bloodless revolution of 24 June 1932 that ended absolute monarchy under King…

khasa-malla-kingdom.s: The Khasa Malla kingdom was a medieval state of western Nepal and adjoining western Tibet, ruled from Sinja in the Karnali basin. At its height in the 13th and 14th centuries its kings raided the Kathmandu Valley and controlled much of the western Himalaya.

khidr-bey-of-teke.s: Khidr Bey was a ruler of the Teke beylik on the southern coast of Anatolia in the first half of the 14th century, with his seat at Antalya. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta met him at Antalya in the early 1330s and described the city and its trade.

kho-orluk.s: Kho Orluk was a leader of the Torghut, an Oirat Mongol people, who led his followers west from Dzungaria across the Kazakh steppe in the early 17th century. By about 1630 they had reached the lower Volga, displacing the Nogai, and founded what became the Kalmyk Khanate.

kholodny-yar.s: Kholodny Yar is a forested area of ravines near Chyhyryn in central Ukraine, around the Motronynskyi Monastery. It is linked in Ukrainian memory with the Cossack Hetmanate and the haidamaka rising of 1768.

khorloogiin-choibalsan.s: Khorloogiin Choibalsan was the leader of the Mongolian People's Republic from the late 1930s until his death in 1952. A founder of the Mongolian People's Party, he became prime minister in 1939 and closely followed Stalin's model.

khuc-hao.s: Khuc Hao was a Vietnamese governor of the Tinh Hai circuit, the former Tang protectorate of Annam, from 907 to 917. Succeeding his father Khuc Thua Du, he ruled autonomously while professing loyalty to Chinese courts, reorganising local administration, taxes and labour service.

khuc-thua-du.s: Khuc Thua Du was a landowner from Hong Chau in the Red River delta who seized control of the Tinh Hai circuit in 905 as the Tang dynasty collapsed. The weakened Tang court recognised him as military governor.

khuman-singh-of-charkhari.s: Khuman Singh was a Bundela Rajput descended from Maharaja Chhatrasal through the Jaitpur branch, who founded the state of Charkhari in Bundelkhand around 1765 on his share of the family lands. His successors were confirmed by the British in 1804, and the state remained a…

khun-borom.s: Khun Borom is the legendary ancestor of the Lao and other Tai peoples in Lao chronicles. According to the tradition, he was sent from heaven to rule at Muang Thaen, near Dien Bien Phu, and his seven sons founded the principalities of the Tai world, among them Muang Sua, later…

khun-chom-tham.s: Khun Chom Tham is the traditional founder of the northern Thai kingdom of Phayao. Northern Thai chronicles describe him as a prince of the Ngoenyang line of Chiang Saen who founded the town on the shore of the lake now called Kwan Phayao in the late 11th century.

khun-lo.s: Khun Lo is the legendary founder of the ruling line of Muang Sua, the town that became Luang Prabang. Lao chronicles describe him as the eldest son of Khun Borom, who took the town from its earlier inhabitants, traditionally in the 8th century.

kido-witbooi.s: Kido Witbooi was the leader of the Witbooi Oorlam, or Khowesin, a Nama-speaking community from the northern Cape. Around 1863 he led them north from Pella to Gibeon in central southern Namibia, where a Rhenish mission was established and the Witboois became one of the leading…

kigeli-iv-rwabugiri.s: Kigeli IV Rwabugiri was mwami (king) of Rwanda in the second half of the 19th century and is regarded as its most powerful pre-colonial ruler. He centralised royal authority, weakened lineage chiefs, extended the system of cattle clientage and led many military campaigns…

kilkenny-castle.s: Kilkenny Castle is a castle above the River Nore in Kilkenny, Ireland, first built for William Marshal in the early 13th century on the site of an earlier Norman fortification. James Butler, 3rd Earl of Ormond, bought it in 1391, and it became the main seat of the Butler earls…

kim-tong-jeong.s: Kim Tong-jeong was a Korean military officer who led the last phase of the Sambyeolcho rebellion against the Goryeo court and its Mongol overlords. After Goryeo and Mongol forces took the rebel base on Jindo in 1271, he withdrew with the survivors to Jeju Island, where they…

kim-tu-bong.s: Kim Tu-bong was a Korean linguist and communist politician who led the Yanan faction of Koreans returning from China in 1945. He was vice chairman of the Provisional People's Committee for North Korea, the first chairman of the Workers' Party of North Korea and later head of…

kim-yu-sin.s: Kim Yu-sin was a Silla general descended from the royal house of Geumgwan Gaya, his great-grandfather being its last king, Guhyeong. He led Silla's armies in the wars that destroyed Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668, alliances made with Tang China, and supported the rise of…

king-cheng-of-chu.s: King Cheng of Chu ruled the southern Chinese state of Chu from 671 to 626 BCE. A son of King Wen of Chu and Xi Gui, the captured lady of Xi, he expanded Chu's power north towards the central plain until his army was defeated by Jin at Chengpu in 632 BCE.

king-huai-of-chu.s: King Huai of Chu ruled the state of Chu from 328 to 299 BCE. Misled by the Qin diplomat Zhang Yi, he broke his alliance with Qi and suffered heavy defeats by Qin.

king-williams-town.s: King William's Town is a town on the Buffalo River in the Eastern Cape of South Africa, founded in 1835 as a military headquarters during the frontier war against the Xhosa and named after King William IV. It was the seat of the short-lived Province of Queen Adelaide and later…

king-yan-of-song.s: King Yan of Song was the last ruler of the state of Song in the Warring States period, taking power around 328 BCE and later assuming the royal title. He fought aggressive wars against his neighbours, conquering the small state of Teng, and Chinese histories portray him as a…

kinich-bahlam-ii.s: K'inich B'ahlam II was a Classic Maya king of Waka', the city now called El Perú, in the north-western Petén of Guatemala, in the late 7th century. He ruled as an ally of the Kaan kingdom of Calakmul and married the Kaan princess Lady K'abel, who held the title of supreme…

kinich-janaab-pakal.s: K'inich Janaab Pakal was king of Palenque from 615 to 683, the most celebrated ruler of the Classic Maya. He restored the city after sacks by Calakmul and built much of the Palace and the Temple of the Inscriptions.

kinich-kan-bahlam-ii.s: K'inich Kan B'ahlam II was king of Palenque from 684 to 702, succeeding his father K'inich Janaab Pakal. He completed his father's funerary temple and built the Cross Group, three temples whose carved panels set out the mythical origins of the dynasty and its patron gods.

kinich-yat-ahk-ii.s: K'inich Yat Ahk II was the last known king of the Classic Maya city of Piedras Negras on the Usumacinta river, ruling from 781. His reign produced fine monuments, including a carved throne.

kirat-singh-of-kishtwar.s: Kirat Singh was a Raja of Kishtwar in the hills east of Kashmir in the 17th century. Under the influence of the Sufi saint Shah Farid-ud-din, he converted to Islam, after which the ruling dynasty and much of the population of Kishtwar became Muslim.

kirat-singh-of-dholpur.s: Kirat Singh was a Jat Rana of Gohad who became the first ruler of the princely state of Dholpur. In 1806 the British returned Gohad and Gwalior to the Scindias and compensated him with Dholpur, Bari and Rajakhera on the Chambal river.

kirtivarman-ii.s: Kirtivarman II was the last king of the Chalukya dynasty of Badami, succeeding his father Vikramaditya II in 746. In 753 his feudatory Dantidurga overthrew him and founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty, which took over the Chalukya lands in the Deccan.

kishan-singh-of-kishangarh.s: Kishan Singh was a Rathore Rajput prince, a son of Raja Udai Singh of Marwar, who founded the state of Kishangarh near Ajmer in 1611 with territory granted by the Mughal emperor Jahangir. The state was named after him.

kiya-afrasiyab.s: Kiya Afrasiyab of the Chelavi family was a commander and in-law of Fakhr al-Dawla Hasan, the last Bavandid ruler of Mazandaran. In 1349 he murdered Hasan and took control of Amol and much of Mazandaran.

knights-templar.s: The Knights Templar were a Catholic military order founded in Jerusalem around 1119 to protect pilgrims in the crusader states. They became a wealthy international organisation with castles, estates and banking operations across Europe and the Levant.

kobayakawa-hideaki.s: Kobayakawa Hideaki was a Japanese daimyo, a nephew of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's wife adopted into the Kobayakawa family. At the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 his defection from the Western army to Tokugawa Ieyasu decided the battle.

kohandil-khan.s: Kohandil Khan was one of the Barakzai Sardars of Kandahar, half-brothers of Dost Mohammad Khan, who ruled the city and its region after the collapse of the Durrani Empire. He led the principality during the First Anglo-Afghan War, when the British occupied Kandahar and he took…

koli-tenguella.s: Koli Tenguella was a Fulani leader who around 1490 led a mass migration of herders and warriors from the Futa Jallon highlands towards the Senegal river. He conquered Futa Toro and founded the Denianke dynasty, which ruled it until the Islamic revolution of 1776.

kondraty-bulavin.s: Kondraty Bulavin was a Don Cossack ataman who led a great revolt against Peter the Great in 1707 and 1708. It began after a punitive expedition sought runaway peasants on the Don and spread among Cossacks, fugitive serfs and the urban poor.

konrad-adenauer.s: Konrad Adenauer was the first Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany, from 1949 to 1963. A former mayor of Cologne removed by the Nazis, he led the Christian Democratic Union and anchored West Germany in the West through NATO membership, reconciliation with France and…

konrad-i-of-masovia.s: Konrad I of Masovia was a Polish duke of the Piast dynasty, ruling Masovia and Kuyavia and briefly holding Kraków. Unable to stop raids by the pagan Prussians, he invited the Teutonic Order to Poland and granted it the Chełmno land around 1226.

konstantin-dragas.s: Konstantin Dragaš was a Serbian magnate who with his brother Jovan ruled a lordship in north-eastern Macedonia, from Kumanovo to Velbazhd and Strumica, after the death of Stefan Dušan. He became an Ottoman vassal and was killed fighting for the Ottomans at the Battle of Rovine…

konstantin-von-neurath.s: Konstantin von Neurath was a German diplomat who served as foreign minister from 1932 to 1938 and then as Reich Protector of Bohemia and Moravia from 1939. Considered too lenient by Hitler, he was replaced in practice by Reinhard Heydrich in 1941.

konstantin-of-rostov.s: Konstantin Vsevolodovich was the eldest son of Vsevolod the Big Nest, prince of Rostov and, after defeating his brothers at the Battle of Lipitsa in 1216, Grand Prince of Vladimir until his death in 1218. Before he died he divided the Rostov lands among his sons, creating the…

konstantinos-karamanlis.s: Konstantinos Karamanlis was a Greek conservative statesman, prime minister from 1955 to 1963 and from 1974 to 1980, and president from 1980 to 1985 and 1990 to 1995. Returning from exile when the military junta collapsed in 1974, he led the transition to democracy known as the…

konstantinos-logothetopoulos.s: Konstantinos Logothetopoulos was a Greek physician and professor of gynaecology who served as the second collaborationist prime minister of Greece under Axis occupation, from December 1942 to April 1943. His government had little authority over the German and Italian occupiers…

korean-war.s: The Korean War began on 25 June 1950 when North Korea invaded South Korea. A United Nations force led by the United States drove the North back towards the Chinese border, and the People's Republic of China then intervened with massive forces.

kost-levytsky.s: Kost Levytsky was a Ukrainian lawyer and politician in Austrian Galicia, a leader of the National Democratic Party and member of the Austrian parliament. In November 1918 he headed the first government of the West Ukrainian People's Republic, the State Secretariat, under…

kota-bharu.s: Kota Bharu is a city near the mouth of the Kelantan river in north-eastern Peninsular Malaysia and the royal capital of the state of Kelantan. Sultan Muhammad II made it the seat of government in the 19th century.
