krittibas-ojha.s: Krittibas Ojha was a Bengali poet who wrote the Krittivasi Ramayan, a free retelling of the Sanskrit Ramayana in Bengali verse, probably in the early fifteenth century. Written in simple language and adding episodes from Bengali devotion, it became the most popular version of…

kul-oba.s: Kul-Oba is a Scythian burial mound near Kerch in eastern Crimea, raised in the fourth century BCE. Excavated in 1830, it contained the stone tomb of a nobleman with his wife and a servant, together with rich gold and electrum objects, among them a vase showing Scythian warriors.

kampong-ayer.s: Kampong Ayer is the water village of Bandar Seri Begawan, the capital of Brunei, made up of houses, schools and mosques built on stilts over the Brunei River and linked by wooden walkways. Antonio Pigafetta, who visited in 1521, described a large city built over the water on…

khuzestan.s: Khuzestan, historically Khuzistan, is a province of south-western Iran at the head of the Persian Gulf, watered by the Karun River. It was the heartland of ancient Elam, with Susa as its chief city, and later a rich province of the Achaemenid, Sasanian and Islamic empires,…

kallinikos.s: Kallinikos was a Greek-speaking architect or engineer from Heliopolis in Syria who, according to the chronicler Theophanes, fled to Constantinople and introduced Greek fire around 672. The incendiary liquid, projected through siphons from ships, helped the Byzantines defeat…

kingdom-of-tylis.s: The Kingdom of Tylis was a Celtic state in eastern Thrace founded by Gauls under Comontorius after the Celtic invasion of the Balkans in 279 BCE. Its kings extracted heavy tribute from Byzantium, which Polybius says rose to 80 talents a year and led to a war over tolls on the…

kaba-ye-zartosht.s: The Ka'ba-ye Zartosht is a square stone tower of the Achaemenid period at Naqsh-e Rostam near Persepolis in Iran; its original purpose is still debated. Its walls carry the long trilingual inscription of the Sasanian king Shapur I, in Middle Persian, Parthian and Greek,…

kailasanathar-temple-kanchipuram.s: The Kailasanathar Temple at Kanchipuram in Tamil Nadu, India, was built around 700 by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, also called Rajasimha. Dedicated to Shiva, it is the oldest structural temple in the city and a key early work of the southern Dravida style.

krasnaya-polyana.s: Krasnaya Polyana is a mountain settlement in the Sochi district of Krasnodar Krai, Russia, on the site of the Circassian locality of Kbaada. There, on 21 May 1864, Russian forces held a victory parade marking the end of the Russo-Circassian War.

kevin-rudd.s: Kevin Rudd was the Labor prime minister of Australia from 2007 to 2010 and again briefly in 2013. His government ratified the Kyoto Protocol, delivered the national apology to the Stolen Generations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children in February 2008, and used…

king-leopolds-soliloquy.s: King Leopold's Soliloquy is a satirical pamphlet by Mark Twain, published in 1905 in support of the Congo Reform Association. Written as a rambling monologue in which Leopold II defends his rule of the Congo Free State, it quotes the evidence against him and includes…

kefe-eyalet.s: Kefe Eyalet was the Ottoman province on the northern coast of the Black Sea, centred on the port of Kefe (Caffa, now Feodosia) in Crimea. Formed from the Genoese colonies and Theodoro, conquered in 1475, it covered the southern coast of Crimea and later fortresses such as…

klement-gottwald.s: Klement Gottwald was leader of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia from 1929. He became prime minister after the party's success in the 1946 elections, led the communist seizure of power in February 1948 and succeeded Edvard Beneš as president that June.

karel-capek.s: Karel Čapek was a Czech writer and journalist of the interwar republic and a friend of President Masaryk. His play R.U.R. of 1920 introduced the word robot, coined by his brother Josef, and his novel War with the Newts satirised fascism and greed.

kosice-programme.s: The Košice Programme was the government programme proclaimed on 5 April 1945 in Košice, in liberated eastern Slovakia, by the new Czechoslovak government of the National Front. Agreed between Edvard Beneš's exiles and the communists in Moscow, it provided for alliance with the…

konrad-henlein.s: Konrad Henlein was the leader of the Sudeten German Party in Czechoslovakia, which he founded in 1933. Acting on Hitler's instructions, he raised demands that the Czechoslovak government could not meet, preparing the Munich Agreement of 1938.

kingdom-of-strathclyde.s: The Kingdom of Strathclyde was a Brittonic kingdom of the early medieval north, centred first on Dumbarton Rock, called Alt Clut, and after a Viking siege of 870 on Govan and the Clyde valley. Its kings fought the Gaels of Dál Riata, the Picts and the Northumbrians.

kells.s: Kells is a town in County Meath in Ireland. A new monastery of the community of Columba was built there in the early ninth century after Viking raids on Iona, and it became the chief house of the Columban monasteries.

kilmartin.s: Kilmartin is a village in Argyll, western Scotland, at the head of Kilmartin Glen, a valley with one of Scotland's densest groups of prehistoric monuments, including chambered cairns, standing stones and rock art. The hillfort of Dunadd, the royal centre of Dál Riata, rises…

kronborg.s: Kronborg is a Renaissance castle at Helsingør on the narrowest point of the Øresund, where Denmark collected the Sound Toll from passing ships. Frederick II rebuilt an earlier fortress there between 1574 and 1585, and Christian IV restored it after a fire in 1629.

kremsmunster-abbey.s: Kremsmünster Abbey is a Benedictine monastery in Upper Austria, founded in 777 by Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria to spread Christianity and settlement on the eastern frontier. Its treasury holds the Tassilo Chalice, a gilded copper chalice given by Tassilo and his wife Liutpirga.

kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.s: The Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia was a crown land of the Austrian Empire created by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 from the former Duchy of Milan and Republic of Venice. Ruled from Milan and Venice under an Austrian viceroy, it was a centre of Italian nationalist opposition and…

kolbacz-abbey.s: Kołbacz Abbey was a Cistercian monastery near Szczecin in Pomerania, founded in 1173 by monks from Esrum in Denmark at the invitation of the Pomeranian noble Wartislaw Świętoborzyc. It became one of the richest monasteries of the duchy and organised German settlement and…

korte-verklaring.s: The Korte Verklaring, or Short Declaration, was a brief standard treaty that the Dutch colonial government required indigenous rulers in the outer islands of the East Indies to sign from 1898. First used in Aceh under J.

kingdom-of-holland.s: The Kingdom of Holland was a monarchy created by Napoleon in 1806 to replace the Batavian Republic, with his brother Louis Bonaparte as king. Louis tried to protect Dutch interests, enforcing the Continental System only loosely, and he sent Herman Willem Daendels to govern Java.

kashgar.s: Kashgar is an oasis city in the far west of Xinjiang, China, near the borders of Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, where Silk Road routes across the Pamirs met those around the Tarim Basin. For centuries a centre of Uyghur Muslim culture and trade, it was ruled by the Karakhanids,…

khara-khula.s: Khara Khula was a chief of the Choros tribe of the Oirats who built up a power base in the steppe between the Altai Mountains and the Ili River in the early seventeenth century. Leading Oirat resistance against the Khalkha Mongols of the Altan Khan line, he laid the…

kardam.s: Kardam was khan of Bulgaria from about 777 to around the turn of the 9th century. He ended a long period of internal strife, and in 792 defeated the Byzantine emperor Constantine VI at Markellai, forcing Byzantium to resume paying tribute.

krefeld-gellep.s: Krefeld-Gellep is a district of Krefeld on the lower Rhine and the site of the Roman fort of Gelduba. Its cemetery, with several thousand burials from the Roman period to the Frankish era, is one of the largest excavated in northern Europe.

klaus-stortebeker.s: Klaus Störtebeker (c. 1360–1401) was a leader of the Victual Brothers, a band of pirates who raided shipping in the Baltic and North Sea around 1400.

kontorhaus-district.s: The Kontorhaus District is an area of large office buildings in central Hamburg, built mainly in the 1920s and 1930s for trading and shipping firms. Its brick buildings, among them the Chilehaus, the Sprinkenhof and the Messberghof, are outstanding examples of Brick…

kateb-yacine.s: Kateb Yacine (1929–1989) was an Algerian writer and dramatist. Arrested as a teenager after the Sétif demonstrations of 1945, he drew on that experience in his novel Nedjma (1956), a founding work of modern Algerian literature in French.

kayes.s: Kayes is a city in western Mali on the Senegal River, capital of the Kayes Region. Developed by the French as a river port and railhead from the 1880s, it was the capital of the colony of French Sudan until the seat moved to Bamako in 1908.

karl-ludwig-sand.s: Karl Ludwig Sand was a German theology student and member of the radical student fraternity movement who stabbed the conservative writer August von Kotzebue to death in Mannheim in March 1819. He was executed in 1820.

kannauj.s: Kannauj is an ancient city on the Ganges in present-day Uttar Pradesh, northern India, known in Sanskrit as Kanyakubja. From the seventh century it was the capital of Harsha and then the prize contested by the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas, and it served as the seat of…

kashf-al-mahjub.s: The Kashf al-Mahjub, or Revelation of the Veiled, is the oldest surviving treatise on Sufism written in Persian, composed in Lahore in the eleventh century by the mystic Ali Hujwiri. It explains Sufi doctrines and practices and gives the lives of earlier saints.

khusrau-shah.s: Khusrau Shah was a sultan of the Ghaznavid dynasty and son of Bahram Shah, reigning from 1157 to 1160. Ghazni had been sacked by the Ghurids and was then lost to Oghuz Turkmen, so he ruled from Lahore over the remaining Ghaznavid lands in the Punjab.

kara-khanid-khanate.s: The Kara-Khanid Khanate was a Turkic dynasty that ruled Central Asia from about the ninth century until 1212, the first Turkic dynasty to convert to Islam in the tenth century. In 999 it took Bukhara and ended the Samanid state, dividing Transoxiana with the Ghaznavids.

karramiyya.s: The Karramiyya were a Sunni religious movement founded by Muhammad ibn Karram, who died in 869, which was strong in Khurasan and the mountains of Afghanistan. Known for asceticism, preaching and missionary activity, and accused by opponents of anthropomorphism, they enjoyed…

khalaj.s: The Khalaj are a Turkic people who lived from the early Middle Ages in the region of Ghazni and southern Afghanistan, serving as soldiers for the Ghaznavids and Ghurids. The Khalji dynasty that ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1290 came from this background.

khokhars.s: The Khokhars are a Punjabi clan and community whose lands lay in the Salt Range and northern Punjab, in present-day Pakistan. In the late twelfth and thirteenth centuries they repeatedly rose against the Ghurids and the Delhi Sultanate, and some sources hold them responsible…

khusrau-malik.s: Khusrau Malik was the last sultan of the Ghaznavid dynasty, ruling from Lahore over the Ghaznavid lands in the Punjab from 1160. After Ghazni passed to the Ghurids, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad attacked the Punjab, and in 1186 he took Lahore and captured Khusrau Malik, who was…

kim-busik.s: Kim Bu-sik was a Korean statesman, general and historian of the Goryeo period. In 1135-1136 he suppressed the rebellion of the monk Myocheong at Pyongyang.

karl-du-thil.s: Karl du Thil was a conservative statesman of the Grand Duchy of Hesse who dominated its government from 1829 until the revolution of 1848. He helped bring Hesse into a customs union with Prussia in 1828, a forerunner of the Zollverein, while suppressing radical and democratic…

konstanty-ostrogski.s: Konstanty Ostrogski was a Ruthenian prince and Grand Hetman of Lithuania. Captured by the Muscovites at Vedrosha in 1500, he escaped and later won many victories over the Tatars and, in 1514, the Battle of Orsha over a larger Muscovite army.

kolomna.s: Kolomna is a city in Moscow Oblast, Russia, near the confluence of the Moskva and Oka rivers, about 110 kilometres south-east of Moscow. First mentioned in 1177, it belonged to the Principality of Ryazan until Daniel of Moscow seized it around 1301, giving Moscow control of…

karpuramanjari.s: Karpuramanjari is a play written in Prakrit by Rajashekhara, court poet of the Gurjara-Pratihara kings at Kannauj, around 900 CE. A light romantic comedy of the type called sattaka, it tells of a king's love for the princess Karpuramanjari and his queen's jealousy.

kavyamimamsa.s: The Kavyamimamsa is a Sanskrit treatise on poetics written by Rajashekhara at the court of Kannauj around 900 CE. Rather than defining figures of speech, it deals with the poet's training, the sources of inspiration, the conduct of literary life and the geography of India as…

kuvalayamala.s: The Kuvalayamala is a Prakrit prose romance by the Jain monk Uddyotana Suri, completed at Jalor in Rajasthan in 778 CE. A complex tale of rebirths meant to teach Jain doctrine, it is also a rich source on the society, languages and commerce of early medieval India, and it…

karlskirche.s: The Karlskirche is a Baroque church in Vienna dedicated to Saint Charles Borromeo, built by Emperor Charles VI in fulfilment of a vow made during the plague of 1713. Designed by Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach and completed by his son Joseph Emanuel between 1716 and 1737,…

kumarbi-cycle.s: The Kumarbi Cycle is a group of Hittite mythological texts of Hurrian origin, preserved on tablets from the Hittite capital Hattusa. It tells how the god Kumarbi overthrew the sky god Anu and was in turn displaced by the storm god Teshub, and in the Song of Ullikummi how he…

kannanur-kuppam.s: Kannanur Kuppam was the second capital of the Hoysala kings in the Tamil country, near Srirangam in present-day Tiruchirappalli district, Tamil Nadu. Vira Someshvara built it in the 13th century to oversee the Hoysala territories along the Kaveri, and his son Ramanatha ruled…

kopperunchinga-i.s: Kopperunchinga I was a chief of the Kadava family who ruled in the northern Tamil country in the early 13th century, as Chola power declined. Around 1231 he captured the Chola king Rajaraja III and held him at Sendamangalam, until the intervention of the Hoysala king Narasimha…

kota-tinggi.s: Kota Tinggi is a town on the Johor River in the Malaysian state of Johor and the seat of the district of the same name. In the seventeenth century it was a royal seat of the Johor Sultanate, and there in 1699 Sultan Mahmud Shah II, the last of the Malacca line, was murdered;…

kim-hong-do.s: Kim Hong-do, known by his pen name Danwon, was a Korean court painter of the late Joseon dynasty who served King Jeongjo. He painted landscapes, Daoist immortals and portraits, but is best known for his genre paintings of ordinary people at work and play, such as wrestlers,…

kukawa.s: Kukawa is a town in Borno State in north-eastern Nigeria, near the western shore of Lake Chad. It was founded in 1814 by the scholar and war leader Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi and became the capital of Bornu under his family.

kalyan-minaret.s: The Kalyan Minaret is a brick minaret in Bukhara, Uzbekistan, built in 1127 by the Kara-Khanid ruler Arslan Khan Muhammad. About 46 metres high and decorated with bands of patterned brickwork, it was the tallest building in Central Asia for centuries.

kabanbay-batyr.s: Kabanbay Batyr was a Kazakh warrior leader (batyr) of the Naiman tribe of the Middle Juz. He was one of the commanders of the Kazakh militias in the eighteenth-century wars against the Dzungars, taking part in the victories at Bulanty and Anyrakai alongside Abulkhair Khan and…

kyiv-pechersk-lavra.s: The Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, or Monastery of the Caves, is an Orthodox monastery in Kyiv founded in 1051 by the monks Anthony and Theodosius in caves above the Dnieper. It became the leading monastery and centre of learning of Kievan Rus', where the Primary Chronicle is…

krivichs.s: The Krivichians were an East Slavic tribal union of the early Middle Ages, living around the upper Dnieper, Western Dvina and Volga, with centres at Smolensk, Polotsk and Izborsk. According to the Primary Chronicle they were among the tribes that invited the Varangians to rule…

kahaya-ii.s: Kahaya II was Omugabe, or king, of Ankole from 1895 to 1944. He was installed young after the succession conflict that followed the death of Ntare V, with the backing of Nuwa Mbaguta, who as chief minister held much of the real power.

kalervo-oberg.s: Kalervo Oberg was a Canadian anthropologist, best known for coining the term "culture shock". His fieldwork in Ankole in the 1930s produced the chapter on the kingdom in the influential collection African Political Systems (1940), which presented Ankole as a state built on the…

kaiserbrief.s: The Kaiserbrief was a letter of November 1870, drafted by Otto von Bismarck and signed by Ludwig II of Bavaria, inviting King William I of Prussia to take the title of German Emperor on behalf of the German princes. Ludwig signed after Bismarck agreed to secret payments to him…

karl-philipp-von-wrede.s: Karl Philipp von Wrede was a Bavarian field marshal. He commanded Bavarian troops alongside Napoleon, including in the Russian campaign of 1812, then negotiated the Treaty of Ried in 1813 by which Bavaria joined the Allies.

karlstejn-castle.s: Karlštejn Castle is a Gothic castle south-west of Prague, founded by Charles IV in 1348. It was built to house the imperial regalia, the crown jewels of Bohemia and the emperor's collection of holy relics.

kabaka-yekka.s: Kabaka Yekka, meaning "the king alone", was a political movement and party founded in Buganda in 1961 to defend the position of the kabaka and the kingdom's autonomy. It allied with Milton Obote's Uganda People's Congress to form the government at independence in 1962, and…

kasubi-tombs.s: The Kasubi Tombs on Kasubi Hill in Kampala are the burial place of four kabakas of Buganda: Mutesa I, Mwanga II, Daudi Chwa II and Mutesa II. The main building, a large domed structure of wood, reed and thatch, was built as Mutesa I's palace in 1882 and became his tomb in 1884.

kyadondo.s: Kyadondo is one of the original core counties of the Kingdom of Buganda, in central Uganda. It contains Kampala and the royal hills of Mengo and Kasubi, as well as Namugongo, so that it has been the political centre of the kingdom since the nineteenth century.

kamurasi.s: Kamurasi was omukama of Bunyoro from around 1852 until his death in 1869. His reign was troubled by civil war among royal claimants and by the arrival of armed ivory and slave traders from Khartoum in the north.

khedive-of-egypt.s: Khedive was the title of the hereditary viceroys of Egypt under Ottoman suzerainty, granted by the sultan to Isma'il Pasha in 1867 and used until 1914. The khedives sought to build an African empire in the Sudan and towards the Great Lakes, employing Europeans such as Samuel…

kitahimbwa.s: Kitahimbwa was omukama of Bunyoro from 1898 to 1902, a young son of Kabalega placed on the throne by the British during his father's resistance. With British officials and Ganda chiefs holding real power, he had little authority, and he was deposed in 1902 in favour of his…

karl-polanyi.s: Karl Polanyi was an Austro-Hungarian economic historian and social theorist, best known for "The Great Transformation" (1944), which argued that the self-regulating market economy was a historical novelty. He held that earlier economies were embedded in social relations, and…

kalmar-war.s: The Kalmar War was fought between Denmark-Norway and Sweden from 1611 to 1613. Christian IV attacked to assert Danish dominance in Scandinavia and to stop Swedish expansion in the Arctic north.

king-james-version.s: The King James Version is the English translation of the Bible commissioned by James I and published in 1611 for use in the Church of England. It was prepared by around fifty scholars working in committees, drawing heavily on William Tyndale's earlier translation.

kartlis-tskhovreba.s: Kartlis Tskhovreba, meaning the Life of Kartli or Life of Georgia, is a collection of medieval Georgian chronicles that forms the main narrative source for the history of Georgia. Written by different authors between the ninth and fourteenth centuries, it runs from legendary…

kostis-palamas.s: Kostis Palamas was a Greek poet, a leading figure of the New Athenian School and of the movement to use spoken demotic Greek in literature. His major works include The Twelve Words of the Gypsy and The King's Flute.

kutaisi-governorate.s: The Kutaisi Governorate was a province of the Russian Empire in western Georgia, created in 1846 with its capital at Kutaisi. It covered the lands of the former kingdom of Imereti together with Mingrelia and Guria, and Kutaisi grew into the second city of Georgia.

killala.s: Killala is a village and small port on Killala Bay in County Mayo, in the west of Ireland, and the seat of an ancient bishopric. On 22 August 1798 a French force under General Jean Humbert landed there to support the rebellion of the United Irishmen; after early success at…

kurkh-monoliths.s: The Kurkh Monoliths are two Assyrian stelae found in 1861 at Kurkh, near Diyarbakır in south-eastern Turkey, and now in the British Museum. One, of Shalmaneser III, describes his campaigns up to 853 BCE, including the Battle of Qarqar, and names 'Ahab the Israelite' with 2,000…

kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.s: The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies was the largest state of pre-unification Italy, formed in 1816 when the Bourbon king Ferdinand I merged the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily. It covered the southern mainland and Sicily, with Naples as its capital.

ketef-hinnom.s: Ketef Hinnom is an archaeological site south-west of the Old City of Jerusalem, where burial caves of the late Iron Age were excavated in 1979. They yielded two tiny rolled silver amulets inscribed with a version of the Priestly Blessing from the Book of Numbers.

khirbet-el-qom.s: Khirbet el-Qom is an archaeological site in the hills west of Hebron, in the West Bank, where tombs of the Iron Age were investigated by William Dever in 1967. A burial inscription of the 8th century BCE found there asks blessing by Yahweh and by his Asherah.

kuntillet-ajrud.s: Kuntillet Ajrud is an archaeological site in north-eastern Sinai, a small way station of around 800 BCE on a desert route between Gaza and the Gulf of Aqaba. Its plastered walls and storage jars carry Hebrew and Phoenician inscriptions, including blessings by Yahweh of Samaria…

kalashoka.s: Kalashoka was a king of Magadha of the Shishunaga dynasty in the 4th century BCE, called Kakavarna in the Puranas. Buddhist tradition says the Second Buddhist Council was held at Vaishali under his patronage, about a century after the death of the Buddha.

kanthirava-narasaraja-i.s: Kanthirava Narasaraja I (1615–1659) was the Wodeyar king of Mysore from 1638 to 1659. He defended his capital Srirangapatna against forces of the Bijapur Sultanate and extended the kingdom at the expense of neighbouring chiefs, making Mysore a significant regional power after…

krishnaraja-wodeyar-ii.s: Krishnaraja Wodeyar II (1728–1766) was king of Mysore from 1734 to 1766. Throughout his reign real power lay with ministers: first the dalavayi Devaraja and his brother Nanjaraja of the Kalale family, and from 1761 the soldier Hyder Ali, who took control of the government.

kot-massacre.s: The Kot massacre took place on the night of 14–15 September 1846 in the Kot, the palace armoury courtyard in Kathmandu. After the murder of a favourite of Queen Rajya Lakshmi, Jang Bahadur Kunwar and his brothers killed dozens of leading nobles and officials, including the…

kyle-ayrshire.s: Kyle is a historic district of central Ayrshire in south-west Scotland, lying between the rivers Irvine and Doon. In the early Middle Ages it was part of the Brittonic north; Eadberht of Northumbria annexed it in 750, extending Northumbrian rule westward.

karlstad.s: Karlstad is a city in Värmland in western Sweden, on the delta of the river Klarälven where it enters Lake Vänern. It received its town charter from Charles IX in 1584 and is named after him.

kongsberg.s: Kongsberg is a town in south-eastern Norway, founded in 1624 by Christian IV after silver was discovered nearby in 1623. The Kongsberg silver mines became the largest industrial enterprise in eighteenth-century Norway and an important source of royal revenue, and the town was…

konungs-skuggsja.s: Konungs skuggsjá (The King's Mirror) is an Old Norse educational work written in Norway around 1250, probably for the sons of King Haakon IV. Framed as a dialogue between a father and son, it gives advice on the conduct of merchants, courtiers and kings, and includes…

krupp.s: Krupp was a German steel and armaments firm founded in Essen in 1811 by Friedrich Krupp. Under his son Alfred it became the leading maker of cast steel and of breech-loading guns, supplying Prussia and many foreign states.

kanjogera.s: Kanjogera was a wife of King Kigeli IV Rwabugiri of Rwanda and a member of the powerful Bega clan. After Rwabugiri's death in 1895 she served as queen mother to the heir Mibambwe IV Rutarindwa, but in 1896 her faction overthrew him in the Coup of Rucunshu and put her own son…

kigeli-v-ndahindurwa.s: Kigeli V Ndahindurwa was the last king of Rwanda, from July 1959 to 1961. A half-brother of Mutara III Rudahigwa, he was installed by court conservatives after Mutara's sudden death.

kingdom-of-main.s: The Kingdom of Ma'in was an ancient South Arabian state of the Minaeans in the Jawf valley of northern Yemen, with its capital at Qarnaw and a religious centre at Yathill (Baraqish). Flourishing roughly from the sixth or fourth century to the first century BCE, it controlled…

kelso-abbey.s: Kelso Abbey is a ruined abbey in the Scottish Borders, founded by Tironensian monks who moved there from Selkirk under David I in 1128. It became one of the richest monasteries in Scotland.

kexholm.s: Kexholm, in Finnish Käkisalmi and today Priozersk in Russia, is a town and fortress on the Vuoksi river near Lake Ladoga, which gave its name to the surrounding province of Kexholm. Sweden won the town and province from Russia by the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617 and held them…

kalmar-union.s: The Kalmar Union was the personal union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden under a single monarch, created through the work of Queen Margaret I and sealed by the coronation of Eric of Pomerania at Kalmar in 1397. Danish dominance provoked repeated Swedish revolts and long periods…

karel-doorman.s: Karel Doorman was a Dutch rear admiral who commanded the combined Allied naval striking force in the Netherlands East Indies in early 1942. On 27 February 1942 his fleet of Dutch, British, American and Australian ships was defeated by a Japanese force in the Battle of the Java…

karmir-blur.s: Karmir Blur is an archaeological site on the outskirts of Yerevan, Armenia, the remains of the Urartian fortress-city of Teishebaini founded by Rusa II in the seventh century BCE. Excavated from 1939 by Boris Piotrovsky, it yielded storerooms holding hundreds of large wine and…

kelishin-stele.s: The Kelishin stele is a Urartian inscribed stone pillar standing on the Kelishin pass, high in the Zagros mountains on the border between Iraq and Iran. Set up around 800 BCE by Ishpuini and his son Menua, it bears a bilingual text in Urartian and Assyrian recording their…

kingdom-of-east-anglia.s: The Kingdom of East Anglia was the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the East Angles, covering modern Norfolk and Suffolk, from the sixth century until 869. Its early king Rædwald was overlord of the southern English, and the Sutton Hoo ship burial is probably his.

korntal.s: Korntal is a town near Stuttgart in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, founded in 1819 by Pietists under Gottlieb Wilhelm Hoffmann with special privileges from King William I. Its independent Brethren congregation, outside the official Lutheran church, made it a model Pietist…

kairatos.s: The Kairatos is a small river in north-central Crete that flows past the Minoan palace of Knossos and reaches the sea east of Heraklion. Its valley gave the Bronze Age palace and the later Greek city of Knossos water and a route to the coast, and the geographer Strabo records…

kanaung-mintha.s: The Kanaung Prince, or Kanaung Mintha, was a Burmese prince, younger brother and heir of King Mindon and the leading reformer of his court. He commanded the army and directed modernisation, sending students abroad and setting up factories and arsenals with European help.

kuthodaw-pagoda.s: The Kuthodaw Pagoda is a Buddhist stupa at the foot of Mandalay Hill in Myanmar, built by King Mindon and completed in 1868. Around it stand 729 small shrines, each sheltering a marble slab inscribed with part of the Pali canon, the Tipitaka, often called the world's largest…

kushano-sasanian-kingdom.s: The Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom was the realm of Sasanian princes who governed Bactria and parts of Gandhara after the Sasanian conquest of the western Kushan lands in the 3rd century CE. Its rulers styled themselves Kushanshah, "king of the Kushans", and issued coins that…

kanishka-stupa.s: The Kanishka stupa was a monumental Buddhist stupa built by the Kushan emperor Kanishka at Shah-ji-ki-Dheri, on the outskirts of Peshawar in Pakistan. The Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang described it as one of the tallest buildings of the ancient world.

ket-klao.s: Ket Klao was a king of Lan Na who ruled from 1525 to 1538 and again from 1543. His reigns were marked by factional struggles among the nobility; he was deposed by his son and later restored, then killed in 1545.

kue-na.s: Kue Na was a king of Lan Na from 1355 to 1385, remembered as a pious and learned ruler. In 1369 he invited the monk Sumana from Sukhothai, who founded at Chiang Mai a monastic lineage derived from Sri Lanka, and he built Wat Suan Dok for him.

khun-people.s: The Khün are a Tai people of the Kengtung area in eastern Shan State, Myanmar. Closely related in language and culture to the people of Lan Na, they use the Tai Tham script for Buddhist texts.

kengtung.s: Kengtung is a town in eastern Shan State, Myanmar, near the borders of Thailand, Laos and China. It was the capital of the largest Shan principality, ruled by Khün princes who traced ties to Lan Na and alternately acknowledged Burmese and Siamese overlords.

kingkitsarat.s: Kingkitsarat was the first king of Luang Phrabang, ruling from 1707 to 1713. A grandson of Sourigna Vongsa, he returned from exile in Sipsong Panna to contest the throne of Lan Xang, and his establishment at Luang Prabang formalised the division of the kingdom into the rival…

kingdom-of-luang-phrabang.s: The Kingdom of Luang Phrabang was the northern Lao kingdom formed when Lan Xang split after the death of Sourigna Vongsa, with its capital at Luang Prabang. It became a tributary of Siam in 1779 and a French protectorate in 1893.

kulottunga-iii.s: Kulottunga III was the last strong king of the Chola Empire, reigning from 1178 to 1218. He campaigned successfully against the Pandyas, sacking Madurai, and against the Hoysalas and the Sinhalese, and built the Kampaharesvara temple at Thirubuvanam.

kissi-people.s: The Kissi are a West African people living where the borders of Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia meet, in Liberia mainly in Lofa County. They speak a Mel language, are known as rice farmers, and are noted for the small stone figures, called pomdo, found in their fields.

kpelle-people.s: The Kpelle are the largest ethnic group of Liberia, living in the central part of the country and in neighbouring Guinea. They speak a Mande language, and their society has long been organised around rice farming, chieftaincies and the Poro and Sande societies.

katoto.s: Katoto is an archaeological site near Bukama in the Upemba Depression of south-eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, on the upper Lualaba. Its Iron Age cemetery, excavated by the Belgian anthropologist Jacques Hiernaux, held graves furnished with pottery, iron tools and…

kazimierz-michalowski.s: Kazimierz Michałowski was a Polish archaeologist and Egyptologist, founder of the Polish school of Mediterranean archaeology. During the UNESCO campaign to save the monuments of Nubia his mission excavated the cathedral of Faras from 1961 to 1964 and rescued its wall paintings…

kyriakos-of-makuria.s: Kyriakos was a king of Makuria in Nubia in the mid-8th century. According to the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria, around 747 he marched into Upper Egypt with a large army to demand the release of the Coptic patriarch, who had been imprisoned by the Umayyad governor,…

kanhoji-angre.s: Kanhoji Angre was the commander of the Maratha navy in the early 18th century, based at Kolaba and the sea forts of the Konkan coast such as Vijaydurg. He seized merchant ships of the English East India Company and other powers that refused his passes and beat off English and…

kremsier-parliament.s: The Kremsier Parliament was the Austrian constituent Reichstag elected in 1848, which met first in Vienna and from November 1848 at Kroměříž (Kremsier) in Moravia. It abolished serfdom and drafted a federal constitution for the Austrian Empire, but Emperor Franz Joseph…

karel-the-elder-of-zerotin.s: Karel the Elder of Žerotín was a Moravian nobleman, scholar and member of the Unity of the Brethren. As leader of the Moravian estates he sided with Archduke Matthias against Emperor Rudolf II in 1608, winning confirmation of their liberties, and served as governor of Moravia…

khnumhotep-ii.s: Khnumhotep II was a nomarch of the Oryx nome in Middle Egypt under the Twelfth Dynasty kings Amenemhat II and Senusret II. His decorated tomb at Beni Hasan records his family's history and shows a caravan of Asiatic traders led by a chieftain named Abisha.

khusobek.s: Khusobek, also called Sobekkhu, was an Egyptian army officer of the Twelfth Dynasty under Senusret III and Amenemhat III. His stele from Abydos records campaigns in Nubia and an expedition by Senusret III to a place called Sekmem, probably Shechem.

kumma.s: Kumma was an Egyptian fortress of the Middle Kingdom on the east bank of the Nile at the Semna gorge, south of the Second Cataract in Lower Nubia, facing the fortress of Semna on the west bank. Built under Senusret III, it helped guard Egypt's southern frontier.

keraites.s: The Keraites were a powerful Turco-Mongol tribal confederation of central Mongolia in the 12th century, many of whom followed the Church of the East. Their ruler Toghrul, known as Ong Khan, was an early patron and ally of Temüjin, the future Genghis Khan, but the two fell out,…

karen-national-union.s: The Karen National Union is a political organisation of the Karen people of Myanmar, founded in 1947. In January 1949 it began an armed rebellion for an independent Karen state, one of the world's longest-running insurgencies, fought by its Karen National Liberation Army.

karl-donitz.s: Karl Dönitz was a German admiral who commanded the U-boat arm in the Battle of the Atlantic and became commander-in-chief of the navy in 1943. Named by Hitler as his successor, he became head of state on 1 May 1945 and authorised the surrender of the German armed forces.

kriegsmarine.s: The Kriegsmarine was the navy of Nazi Germany from 1935 to 1945, successor to the Reichsmarine. Much smaller than the Royal Navy, it relied in the Second World War on surface raiders and above all on U-boats, which sank thousands of Allied merchant ships in the Battle of the…

kayforce.s: Kayforce was the New Zealand Army force raised for service in the Korean War under the United Nations Command. Formed in 1950 around the 16th Field Regiment of artillery, it served with the 1st Commonwealth Division from 1951, notably supporting the Battle of Kapyong.

keith-holyoake.s: Keith Holyoake was a New Zealand farmer and politician of the National Party who was Prime Minister briefly in 1957 and again from 1960 to 1972, one of the longest tenures in the country's history. His government presided over prosperity, sent forces to the Vietnam War and…

khai-dinh.s: Khải Định was emperor of Vietnam of the Nguyen dynasty from 1916 to 1925, under the French protectorate. Placed on the throne after the exile of Duy Tân, he cooperated closely with the colonial authorities and visited France in 1922, drawing criticism from nationalists such as…

kazanlak-tomb.s: The Thracian Tomb of Kazanlak is a beehive-shaped brick tomb near Kazanlak in central Bulgaria, discovered in 1944 and dated to around 300 BCE. Its corridor and burial chamber are decorated with well-preserved wall paintings of a funeral feast, a chariot race and Thracian…

koffiefontein.s: Koffiefontein is a small town in the south-west of the Free State province of South Africa, founded after diamonds were found there in 1870. Its diamond mine, worked from the 1870s, was one of the deposits that remained in the Orange Free State after Britain annexed Griqualand…

kyansittha.s: Kyansittha was king of Pagan from 1084 to about 1112, one of the most celebrated rulers of the Pagan Kingdom. A general of Anawrahta, he crushed the rebellion of Nga Yaman Kan in which King Sawlu was killed and then took the throne.

kyaswa-of-pagan.s: Kyaswa was king of Pagan from 1235 to 1251, the son and successor of Htilominlo. Remembered as a learned and pious king devoted to the study of Buddhist scripture, he left government largely to his ministers and gained little new territory or revenue.

kadam-school.s: The Kadam school was a tradition of Tibetan Buddhism founded in the eleventh century by Dromtön, a disciple of the Indian teacher Atisha, who established Reting Monastery in 1056. It stressed monastic discipline and the graded path to enlightenment.

khalimpur-copper-plate.s: The Khalimpur copper plate is a land grant of the Pala king Dharmapala, found at Khalimpur in the Malda district of West Bengal. It is the main source for the origins of the Pala dynasty, describing the anarchy before Gopala as matsyanyaya, 'the law of the fish', and recording…

kadava-dynasty.s: The Kadava dynasty was a line of chieftains in northern Tamil Nadu who claimed descent from the Pallavas and served as feudatories of the Cholas. In the thirteenth century, under Kopperunchinga I and his son Kopperunchinga II, they took advantage of Chola weakness to rule an…

kanchipuram.s: Kanchipuram is a city in northern Tamil Nadu, India, on the Vegavathi river, counted among the seven sacred cities of Hinduism. It was the capital of the Pallava dynasty from about the fourth to the ninth century and a centre of Sanskrit, Buddhist and Jain learning, and later…

kiliya.s: Kiliya, Chilia in Romanian, is a town on the Chilia branch of the Danube delta in Ukraine. A medieval trade port contested by Hungary, Wallachia and Moldavia, it was taken by Stephen the Great in 1465 and by the Ottomans in 1484, cutting Moldavia off from the sea.

khotyn.s: Khotyn, Hotin in Romanian, is a town on the Dniester in western Ukraine, known for its medieval fortress. A Moldavian stronghold, it was the site of battles in 1621 and 1673 between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Ottomans, and passed to Russia in 1812.

khottiga.s: Khottiga was Rashtrakuta emperor of the Deccan from 967 to 972, succeeding his brother Krishna III. His reign saw the rapid decline of the empire: in 972 the Paramara king Siyaka II of Malwa, a former vassal, invaded the Deccan and sacked the capital Manyakheta.

krishna-ii-rashtrakuta.s: Krishna II was Rashtrakuta emperor of the Deccan from about 878 to 914, the son and successor of Amoghavarsha I. His reign was taken up by wars with the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi and the Gurjara-Pratiharas of northern India, some of which went badly, although he kept control…

kanchanaburi.s: Kanchanaburi is a town in western Thailand at the meeting of the Khwae Noi and Khwae Yai rivers, capital of the province of the same name. It guarded the route from Burma through the Three Pagodas Pass, used by Burmese armies in the wars of the eighteenth century.

kouloughlis.s: The Kouloughlis were the sons of Ottoman soldiers, mostly Janissaries, and local North African women in the Regencies of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli. In Algiers they were gradually excluded from the Janissary corps and high office to preserve the power of soldiers recruited…

konstantin-konik.s: Konstantin Konik was an Estonian surgeon and politician. In February 1918 he was one of the three members of the Salvation Committee, with Konstantin Päts and Jüri Vilms, which issued the Manifesto to the Peoples of Estonia proclaiming independence.

kargil-war.s: The Kargil War was an armed conflict between India and Pakistan from May to July 1999 in the Kargil district, then part of the state of Jammu and Kashmir. Pakistani soldiers and militants had occupied high positions on the Indian side of the Line of Control; the Indian army…

kesavananda-bharati-v-state-of-kerala.n: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
kesavananda-bharati-v-state-of-kerala.s: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala was a case decided by a thirteen-judge bench of the Supreme Court of India in April 1973.

keiko-fujimori.s: Keiko Fujimori is a Peruvian politician, the daughter of Alberto Fujimori, who served as Peru's first lady in the 1990s after her parents separated. As leader of the right-wing Popular Force party she was narrowly defeated in the presidential run-offs of 2011, 2016 and 2021,…

konavle.s: Konavle is a fertile region and municipality at the southern tip of Croatia, between Cavtat and the Bay of Kotor, bordering Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro. The Republic of Ragusa bought it from Bosnian nobles in two stages, in 1419 and 1427, gaining its main source of…

kulmiye.s: Kulmiye (Peace, Unity and Development Party) is a political party in Somaliland founded in 2002 by Ahmed Mohamed Mohamoud (Silanyo). It won the presidential elections of 2010 and 2017, with Silanyo and then Muse Bihi Abdi, and governed until its defeat by the Waddani party in…

kgalema-motlanthe.s: Kgalema Motlanthe is a South African politician who was president of South Africa from September 2008 to May 2009, after the ANC recalled Thabo Mbeki. A former trade unionist and ANC secretary-general, he served as a caretaker until the 2009 election and was then deputy…

kaunghmudaw-pagoda.s: The Kaunghmudaw Pagoda is a large Buddhist stupa near Sagaing in Myanmar, built by King Thalun of the Restored Toungoo dynasty between 1636 and 1648. Its great dome, modelled according to tradition on Sri Lankan stupas, enshrines relics believed to include a tooth of the Buddha.

kiek-in-de-kok.s: Kiek in de Kök is an artillery tower in the town wall of Tallinn (Reval), built from about 1475 and later heightened. Its Low German name, "peep into the kitchen", came from the joke that from its upper floors the guards could see into the kitchens of the houses below.

karpathos.s: Karpathos is a mountainous Greek island in the south-eastern Aegean Sea, between Rhodes and Crete, now part of the Dodecanese. In the Hellenistic period it was ruled by Rhodes, and it later passed through Byzantine, Venetian, Ottoman and Italian rule before joining Greece…

karanis.s: Karanis was a farming town in the north-east of the Faiyum in Egypt, founded in the third century BCE under the Ptolemies and inhabited until late antiquity. Excavations by the University of Michigan from 1924 uncovered houses, granaries, temples and thousands of papyri and…

karashahr.s: Karashahr, called Yanqi in Chinese sources, is an oasis town in the Tarim Basin in Xinjiang, north-western China. In antiquity it was the centre of a Tocharian-speaking Buddhist city state on the northern Silk Road between Turfan and Kucha.

kronstadt-rebellion.s: The Kronstadt rebellion was a revolt in March 1921 by sailors, soldiers and workers of the naval fortress of Kronstadt near Petrograd against the Bolshevik government. Once celebrated supporters of the revolution, the rebels demanded freely elected soviets, freedom of speech…

kabayama-hisataka.s: Kabayama Hisataka was a samurai of the Shimazu clan of Satsuma who commanded the invasion of the Ryukyu Kingdom in 1609. With about 3,000 men he took the Amami Islands and Nakijin Castle and then advanced on Shuri, where King Shō Nei surrendered.

kikaijima.s: Kikaijima is a small island of the Amami group, east of Amami Ōshima, now in Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan. It resisted the expansion of the Ryukyu Kingdom until King Shō Toku sent an expedition in 1466 that brought it under Shuri's control.

karla-caves.s: The Karla Caves are a complex of rock-cut Buddhist monuments near Lonavala in Maharashtra, India. Their Great Chaitya, cut around the first century CE, is the largest and finest early Buddhist prayer hall in India, with a vaulted nave, carved pillars and a stupa.

kalyan.s: Kalyan is a city in Thane district, Maharashtra, India, on the Ulhas river north-east of Mumbai. In antiquity it was a port linking the Deccan with western trade, mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea and in donors' inscriptions in the Kanheri and Nashik caves.

kanva-dynasty.s: The Kanva dynasty ruled Magadha in northern India after the Shungas, traditionally for forty-five years in the first century BCE. Its founder Vasudeva Kanva, a Brahmin minister, killed the last Shunga king Devabhuti, and the dynasty had four kings.

kshaharata-dynasty.s: The Kshaharata were a dynasty of Western Satraps, of Saka origin, who ruled in western India in the first and early second centuries CE. Their greatest ruler, Nahapana, held much of the western Deccan, including Nashik and the ports of the Konkan, as cave inscriptions of his…

kaliman-asen-i.s: Kaliman Asen I was tsar of Bulgaria from 1241 to 1246, succeeding his father Ivan Asen II as a boy of about seven. His regents paid tribute to the Mongols after their raids of 1242 and could not stop losses to the Empire of Nicaea.

kilifarevo-monastery.s: Kilifarevo Monastery is a Bulgarian Orthodox monastery near Veliko Tarnovo, founded around 1350 by the Hesychast monk Theodosius of Tarnovo with the support of Tsar Ivan Alexander. It became a major centre of learning and translation where scholars such as Euthymius were trained.

khalid-bin-muhammad-al-qasimi.s: Khalid bin Muhammad Al Qasimi was ruler of Sharjah from 1965 to 1972, appointed after the British deposed his cousin Saqr bin Sultan. He took part in the negotiations that created the United Arab Emirates, which Sharjah joined in December 1971, and agreed with Iran on shared…

khor-fakkan.s: Khor Fakkan is a port town on the Gulf of Oman coast of the United Arab Emirates, an exclave of the emirate of Sharjah. It was sacked by the Portuguese under Afonso de Albuquerque in 1507 and later came under Qasimi rule.

khaqani.s: Khaqani was a Persian poet from Shirvan, in present-day Azerbaijan, and one of the masters of the Persian ode. He served as court poet to the Shirvanshahs Manuchihr III and Akhsitan I, was imprisoned for a time, and wrote verses from prison as well as a famous ode on the ruins…

kim-alji.s: Kim Alji is the legendary ancestor of the Kim royal clan of Silla. According to the Samguk sagi, in 65 CE, under King Talhae, he was found as a baby in a golden box hanging from a tree in the Gyerim forest at Gyeongju, where a white rooster crowed.

kim-daeseong.s: Kim Daeseong was a chief minister of Silla under King Gyeongdeok. In 751 he began the building of the Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram cave shrine near Gyeongju, according to legend for the parents of his present and his former life.

kim-heonchang.s: Kim Heonchang was a member of the Silla royal family and governor of Ungju, around present-day Gongju. Angered that his father had been passed over for the throne, in 822 he rebelled and proclaimed a new state called Jangan, winning support in several provinces.

kilo-class-submarine.s: The Kilo class is the NATO name for a type of diesel-electric attack submarine designed in the Soviet Union and built from the early 1980s, later in an improved version known as Project 636. Quiet and relatively cheap, it has been exported to many navies, including those of…

koos-de-la-rey.s: Koos de la Rey was a Boer general of the South African Republic and one of the most successful commanders of the Second Boer War. He fought at Modder River and Magersfontein in 1899 and, after the fall of Pretoria, led a long guerrilla campaign in the western Transvaal,…

kgb.s: The KGB (Committee for State Security) was the main security agency of the Soviet Union from 1954 until 1991, responsible for foreign intelligence, counter-intelligence, border troops and the suppression of political dissent. It succeeded the security services descended from…

king-dao-of-chu.s: King Dao of Chu ruled the State of Chu from 401 to 381 BCE. He appointed the general and statesman Wu Qi, who reorganised the government, cut the privileges of distant royal kin and officials and strengthened the army, bringing Chu military successes.

king-fuchu-of-chu.s: King Fuchu was the last king of the State of Chu, reigning from 227 to 223 BCE. In 225 BCE his armies under Xiang Yan routed the Qin invasion led by Li Xin, but the next year a much larger Qin force under Wang Jian defeated Chu, and in 223 BCE Fuchu was captured and the…

king-wei-of-chu.s: King Wei of Chu ruled the State of Chu from 339 to 329 BCE, a time when it was at the height of its territorial power. He defeated the State of Yue in the east, traditionally dated to about 334 BCE, extending Chu to the sea, and defeated Qi at Xuzhou in 333 BCE.

king-zhao-of-zhou.s: King Zhao of Zhou was the fourth king of the Western Zhou dynasty, reigning in the late tenth century BCE. He led campaigns south against Chu and other peoples of the Han River region, recorded in bronze inscriptions.

king-an-of-zhou.s: King An of Zhou was a king of the Eastern Zhou dynasty, reigning from 401 to 376 BCE, when royal power had become largely ceremonial. His reign is remembered for his formal recognition in 386 BCE of Tian He as ruler of the State of Qi, legitimising the Tian clan's usurpation…

kaogong-ji.s: The Kaogong ji is an ancient Chinese technical treatise on crafts, preserved as the last section of the Rites of Zhou in place of a lost chapter. It describes some thirty trades, including chariot building, bronze casting with set alloy proportions, weapon making and the plan…

king-wei-of-qi.s: King Wei of Qi was a ruler of the State of Qi from the Tian family in the fourth century BCE. He reformed the government with the minister Zou Ji, and his armies, led by Tian Ji with the strategist Sun Bin, defeated Wei at Guiling and Maling.

king-xiang-of-zhou.s: King Xiang of Zhou was king of the Eastern Zhou dynasty from 651 to 619 BCE. Early in his reign he honoured Duke Huan of Qi as hegemon at the covenant of Kuiqiu.

king-zhaoxiang-of-qin.s: King Zhaoxiang of Qin ruled the State of Qin from 306 to 251 BCE, the longest reign of the Warring States period. With the minister Fan Ju and the general Bai Qi, he won great victories over Han, Wei, Chu and Zhao, notably at Changping in 260 BCE.

king-huiwen-of-qin.s: King Huiwen of Qin ruled the State of Qin from 338 to 311 BCE. He had the reformer Shang Yang executed on his accession but kept his laws, and in 325 BCE became the first Qin ruler to take the title of king.

komtur.s: Komtur, from Latin commendator, was the title of the commander of a commandery (Komturei) in the Teutonic Order and some other military orders. In Prussia each Komtur governed a district from a castle with a convent of knight-brothers, collecting rents, administering justice…

kamphaeng-phet.s: Kamphaeng Phet is a town on the Ping River in north-central Thailand, known in the fourteenth century as Chakangrao. A fortified frontier town of the Sukhothai kingdom, it was besieged by Ayutthaya in the 1370s and later became an Ayutthayan provincial centre.

karatay-madrasa.s: The Karatay Madrasa is a Seljuk theological college in Konya, Turkey, founded in 1251 by the emir Jalal al-Din Karatay. It is known for its marble portal and for the turquoise and black tile mosaic covering the dome of its central hall.

kaykaus-i.s: Kaykaus I was sultan of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum from 1211 to 1220. He expanded the sultanate to the Black Sea, taking the port of Sinop in 1214 and capturing Emperor Alexios I of Trebizond, whom he released as a tributary.

kaykaus-ii.s: Kaykaus II was sultan of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum from 1246, under Mongol overlordship, sharing or disputing the throne with his brothers Kilij Arslan IV and Kayqubad II. Pressed by the Mongols and his rivals, he fled to the Byzantine Empire in 1261 and later to the Golden…

kaykhusraw-ii.s: Kaykhusraw II was sultan of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum from 1237 to 1246, succeeding his father Kayqubad I. His reign saw the Babai revolt of Turkmen in 1239–1240 and, in 1243, a crushing defeat by the Mongols under Baiju at the Battle of Köse Dağ, after which the sultanate…

kilij-arslan-iv.s: Kilij Arslan IV was sultan of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum from 1248, under Mongol overlordship, at first alongside his brothers Kaykaus II and Kayqubad II. Backed by the Mongols, he became sole ruler after Kaykaus II fled in 1261, but real power lay with the minister known as…

kubadabad-palace.s: Kubadabad Palace was a summer palace of the Seljuk sultans of Rum on the south-western shore of Lake Beyşehir in Turkey, built for Kayqubad I in the 1230s. Excavations have uncovered its halls and many glazed tiles with figures of people, animals and mythical creatures, now…

khalid-bin-barghash.s: Khalid bin Barghash was a son of Sultan Barghash who seized the palace in Zanzibar on the death of Sultan Hamad bin Thuwaini in August 1896 without British approval. On 27 August British warships bombarded the palace in the Anglo-Zanzibar War, which lasted less than an hour.

khalifa-bin-harub.s: Khalifa bin Harub was Sultan of Zanzibar from 1911 to 1960, under the British protectorate. Real power lay with the British resident, but during his long reign he was a respected figurehead and symbol of continuity, while the economy rested on cloves and the Arab landed elite.

karim-ul-makhdum.s: Karim ul-Makhdum was an Arab or Persian Muslim missionary who, according to Sulu tradition, arrived in the Sulu archipelago in the late fourteenth century, traditionally in 1380, and helped spread Islam there. He is credited with founding the mosque at Tubig Indangan on…

kebon-kopi-ii-inscription.s: The Kebon Kopi II inscription is a stone inscription found near Bogor in western Java, Indonesia, written in Old Malay and generally read as dated 932 CE. It records that a king of Sunda had been restored to power, making it the earliest securely dated record naming the Sunda…

kidung-sunda.s: The Kidung Sunda is a Middle Javanese poem preserved in Bali, probably composed in the sixteenth century. It tells the story of the Battle of Bubat of 1357, in which King Linggabuana of Sunda and his daughter Dyah Pitaloka, who was to marry Hayam Wuruk of Majapahit, were…

kalina-people.s: The Kalina, also called Caribs or Galibi, are an Indigenous people of the coastal Guianas and Venezuela who speak a Cariban language. They were among the peoples who fought and traded with the first European colonists in Suriname, and in 1686 Governor Van Aerssen made peace…

keti-koti.s: Keti Koti, Sranan Tongo for "the chain is cut", is the annual commemoration on 1 July of the abolition of slavery in Suriname and the Dutch Caribbean on 1 July 1863. The formerly enslaved were still required to work on plantations under state supervision for a further ten years.

koloniale-staten.s: The Koloniale Staten was the colonial legislature of Suriname, established in 1866. Most of its members were elected by a small electorate qualified by income and education, the rest appointed by the governor, so that it represented a narrow wealthy class.

kagera-salient.s: The Kagera Salient is a strip of Tanzanian territory north of the Kagera River, west of Lake Victoria and bordering Uganda. Idi Amin's Ugandan army invaded and annexed it in late 1978, provoking the Uganda–Tanzania War, in which Tanzanian forces drove out the invaders and went…

katsushika-hokusai.s: Katsushika Hokusai was a Japanese painter and ukiyo-e printmaker of the late Edo period. His series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, published from about 1831 and including The Great Wave off Kanagawa, made the landscape print a major genre, and his sketchbooks, the Hokusai…

kaitai-shinsho.s: The Kaitai Shinsho ('New Text on Anatomy') is a Japanese translation of a Dutch edition of the German physician Johann Adam Kulmus's anatomical tables, published in 1774 by Sugita Genpaku, Maeno Ryōtaku and their colleagues. The first full translation of a Western medical work…

kuzma-minin.s: Kuzma Minin was a meat trader and elected elder of Nizhny Novgorod who in 1611 called on his fellow townspeople to raise money and an army against the Polish occupation of Moscow. With Prince Dmitry Pozharsky as military commander, this Second Volunteer Army freed Moscow in…

kayastha.s: The Kayasthas are a group of Hindu castes of northern and central India traditionally associated with writing, record-keeping and administration. Scribes and accountants in the service of Hindu kingdoms from early medieval times, they also served the Delhi Sultanate, the…

khizr-khan-khalji-prince.s: Khizr Khan was the eldest son of the Delhi sultan Alauddin Khalji and for years his designated heir. After Alauddin took Chittor in 1303, the fort was renamed Khizrabad and placed under him.

krishna-kumari.s: Krishna Kumari was a princess of Mewar, daughter of Maharana Bhim Singh. Her hand was sought by the rulers of Jaipur and Jodhpur, and their rivalry over the betrothal led to a ruinous war in which the Pindari leader Amir Khan and Maratha armies also intervened.

kumbhalgarh.s: Kumbhalgarh is a hill fort in the Aravalli Range north of Udaipur, built in the mid-fifteenth century by Rana Kumbha of Mewar. Its walls, more than 30 km long, enclose many temples, and the fort served as a refuge for the rulers of Mewar: Udai Singh II was hidden there as a…

kizza-besigye.s: Kizza Besigye is a Ugandan physician and politician who served as Yoweri Museveni's personal doctor during the Bush War and rose to colonel in the National Resistance Army. After breaking with Museveni he challenged him in four presidential elections, in 2001, 2006, 2011 and…

kisangani.s: Kisangani is a city on the Congo River in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, at the head of navigation below the Boyoma Falls. Founded by Henry Morton Stanley in 1883 as Stanley Falls station and later called Stanleyville, it was a centre of the Simba…

kliptown.s: Kliptown is one of the oldest residential districts of Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg. On 25–26 June 1955 it hosted the Congress of the People, where the ANC and its allies in the Congress Alliance adopted the Freedom Charter before police broke up the meeting.

khalifa-bin-zayed-al-nahyan.s: Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan was ruler of Abu Dhabi and president of the United Arab Emirates from November 2004 until his death in May 2022, succeeding his father Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan. Formerly crown prince and chairman of the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, he presided…

koloksha.s: The Koloksha is a river in Vladimir Oblast, Russia, a left tributary of the Klyazma. In 1177 Vsevolod the Big Nest defeated Gleb of Ryazan and his allies on its banks and took Gleb prisoner, a victory that secured Vsevolod's hold on the grand principality of Vladimir and…

kalamukha.s: The Kalamukhas were a Shaiva ascetic sect of medieval India, closely related to the Pashupatas, that flourished especially in Karnataka between the ninth and thirteenth centuries. Their priests ran large temples and monastic colleges, such as those at Balligave, teaching…

kasivisvesvara-temple-lakkundi.s: The Kasivisvesvara Temple is a Hindu temple at Lakkundi in Gadag district, Karnataka, built in the late Western Chalukya period, probably in the twelfth century. Dedicated to Shiva, it is celebrated for the exceptionally fine and dense carving of its doorways and outer walls…

king-kang-of-zhou.s: King Kang of Zhou was the third king of the Western Zhou dynasty, the son of King Cheng, traditionally reigning in the late eleventh and early tenth centuries BCE. His reign, with his father's, was later idealised as the 'Peace of Cheng and Kang', when the realm was stable and…

king-xie-of-zhou.s: King Xie of Zhou, personal name Yuchen, was a rival king set up after the fall of the Western Zhou capital in 771 BCE, in opposition to King Ping. Supported by the Duke of Guo and other lords, he ruled for some years at Xie, but around 750 BCE Marquis Wen of Jin killed him,…

khalchayan.s: Khalchayan is an archaeological site in the Surkhandarya region of southern Uzbekistan, excavated by Galina Pugachenkova from 1959. A hall or palace there was decorated with painted clay sculptures of nomad rulers, warriors and deities in Hellenistic style, dated to around the…

kwabulawayo.s: KwaBulawayo was the royal capital of the Zulu king Shaka in the 1820s, near modern Eshowe in KwaZulu-Natal. A great circular military kraal holding thousands of huts and the cattle of the king's regiments, it was visited by the first British traders from Port Natal in 1824.

korcula.s: Korčula is a Croatian island in the southern Adriatic, the Greek Korkyra Melaina ('Black Corfu'). In the early Middle Ages it belonged to the Narentines of Pagania, and it later passed between Croatia-Hungary, Venice and other powers before long Venetian rule from 1420.

ki-hajar-dewantara.s: Ki Hajar Dewantara, born Raden Mas Soewardi Soerjaningrat into the Pakualaman princely family of Yogyakarta, was an Indonesian nationalist and educator. Exiled by the Dutch for his writings, he founded the Taman Siswa school movement in 1922 and became independent Indonesia's…

kamares-ware.s: Kamares ware is a fine Minoan pottery of the Protopalatial period on Crete, named after the Kamares cave on Mount Ida where it was first found. Made on the wheel with walls as thin as eggshell, it is painted in white, red and orange on a dark ground with spirals and plant motifs.

kommos.s: Kommos is a Minoan harbour town on the south coast of Crete, at the edge of the Mesara plain, which probably served as the port of Phaistos. Excavated by Joseph Shaw from 1976, it has large stone buildings, ship sheds and imported pottery from Egypt, Cyprus and the Levant, and…

kuto-besak.s: Kuto Besak is a walled brick palace-fortress (kraton) on the Musi River in Palembang, Sumatra, completed in 1797 for the Sultanate of Palembang. It served as the residence of the sultans until the Dutch conquest in 1821, after which it was used as a military fort; it still…

kuk-bahlam-i.s: K'uk' B'ahlam I was the founder of the royal dynasty of Palenque, the Maya city in Chiapas, Mexico. According to later inscriptions he took power in 431 CE as ruler of the B'aakal kingdom, and the kings of Palenque, including K'inich Janaab Pakal, counted their descent from him.

kampilya.s: Kampilya was an ancient city of northern India, described in the Mahabharata as the capital of southern Panchala and the seat of King Drupada. It is usually identified with Kampil in Farrukhabad district of Uttar Pradesh, near the Ganges.

kshemagupta.s: Kshemagupta was king of Kashmir from 950 to 958, the son of the dynasty's founder Parvagupta. Kalhana's Rajatarangini portrays him as devoted to hunting and pleasure.

karbeas.s: Karbeas was a Byzantine officer who became leader of the Paulicians after Empress Theodora's persecution of the sect around 843, in which his father was put to death. With thousands of followers he fled to the emir of Melitene and founded the fortress of Tephrike, from which…

kurya.s: Kurya was a khan of the Pechenegs, the Turkic nomads of the steppe north of the Black Sea. In 972 his warriors ambushed Prince Sviatoslav I of Kiev at the Dnieper rapids as he returned from his war against Byzantium, and killed him.

kampuchean-united-front-for-national-sal.n: Kampuchean United Front for National Salvation
kampuchean-united-front-for-national-sal.s: The Kampuchean United Front for National Salvation was a movement of Cambodian communists opposed to the Khmer Rouge, founded under Vietnamese sponsorship in December 1978. Its leaders, among them Heng Samrin, Chea Sim and Hun Sen, were former Khmer Rouge cadres who had fled…

kinta-valley.s: The Kinta Valley is a valley of the Kinta river in Perak, Malaysia, around the city of Ipoh. From the late 19th century it was one of the richest tin-mining districts in the world, worked largely by Chinese miners and later by European dredging companies.

kuala-kangsar.s: Kuala Kangsar is a town on the Perak River in Perak, Malaysia, and the royal seat of the sultans of Perak. It was the site of the first Durbar, the conference of Malay rulers of the Federated Malay States, in 1897.

kestros.s: The Kestros, now the Aksu Çayı, is a river of southern Turkey that flows from the Taurus Mountains through the plain of ancient Pamphylia into the Mediterranean east of Antalya. In antiquity it was navigable up to the area of Perge, which lay a short distance from its bank and…

kagyu.s: Kagyu is one of the main schools of Tibetan Buddhism, tracing its teaching lineage from the Indian masters Tilopa and Naropa through the Tibetans Marpa, Milarepa and Gampopa in the 11th and 12th centuries. Gampopa's disciples founded several sub-schools, including the Karma…

kham-fu.s: Kham Fu was a king of Lan Na in northern Thailand in the 1330s, a descendant of the founder Mangrai. Northern Thai chronicles credit him with annexing the neighbouring kingdom of Phayao around 1338, adding its lands to Lan Na.

kwan-phayao.s: Kwan Phayao is a large freshwater lake beside the town of Phayao in northern Thailand. It is the largest freshwater lake of the north and an important fishery.

kyawswa-i-of-pinya.s: Kyawswa I was king of Pinya in central Burma from 1344 to 1350, a son of Thihathu, founder of the kingdom. His reign fell in a period of rivalry between Pinya and the breakaway kingdom of Sagaing, ruled by his half-brother's line.

kyi-shchek-and-khoryv.s: Kyi, Shchek and Khoryv are three legendary brothers who, with their sister Lybid, are credited in the Primary Chronicle with founding Kiev on the hills above the Dnieper. Kyi, the eldest, gave the city its name, and the chronicle names hills and the Lybid river after the others.

kalinga-magha.s: Kalinga Magha was an invader from Kalinga, in eastern India, who conquered northern Sri Lanka and ruled from Polonnaruwa from 1215 to about 1236. Sinhalese chronicles portray his rule as harsh and destructive to Buddhism.

kissamos.s: Kissamos is a town on the Gulf of Kissamos in north-western Crete, Greece, also known as Kastelli. In antiquity Kisamos served as the harbour of the hill city of Polyrrhenia and later became a city in its own right, with a bishopric in Roman and Byzantine times.

kwidzyn.s: Kwidzyn, German Marienwerder, is a town in northern Poland near the lower Vistula. The Teutonic Order founded a castle there in 1233 during its conquest of Pomesania, and it became the seat of the cathedral chapter of the Bishopric of Pomesania, whose brick Gothic castle and…

kadriah-palace.s: The Kadriah Palace is the wooden palace of the sultans of Pontianak in West Kalimantan, Indonesia, at the meeting of the Kapuas and Landak rivers. It was begun in 1771 by Syarif Abdurrahman Alkadrie, founder of the city and sultanate, near his Jami mosque.

kapuas-river.s: The Kapuas is the longest river in Indonesia, flowing about 1,140 kilometres west across West Kalimantan on Borneo to the South China Sea. Pontianak stands near its mouth, and the river has long been the main route into the interior, carrying gold, forest products and later…

karamchand-gandhi.s: Karamchand Gandhi was an Indian administrator, father of Mohandas Gandhi. Like his father Uttamchand, he served as diwan, the chief minister, of the princely state of Porbandar in Kathiawar, and later as diwan of Rajkot and Vankaner.

kirti-mandir-porbandar.s: Kirti Mandir is a memorial in Porbandar, Gujarat, built beside the ancestral house where Mohandas Gandhi was born in 1869. Completed in 1950, it houses an exhibition on the lives of Gandhi and his wife Kasturba.

kochi.s: Kochi, historically Cochin, is a port city in Kerala on the Malabar Coast of India. It rose as a harbour after a flood of 1341 opened its natural channel and became capital of the Kingdom of Cochin.

kristang.s: The Kristang are a Eurasian community of Malacca in Malaysia and of Singapore, descended from Portuguese settlers of the 16th and 17th centuries who married local women. They are mostly Roman Catholic and speak, or once spoke, Papia Kristang, a Portuguese-based creole.

ksar-es-seghir.s: Ksar es-Seghir is a small coastal town on the Strait of Gibraltar in northern Morocco, between Tangier and Ceuta. A medieval port for crossings to Spain, it was captured by Portugal under Afonso V in 1458 and held until 1550.

kaaba.s: The Kaaba is a cube-shaped building at the centre of the Great Mosque of Mecca, the holiest site in Islam. Before Islam it was a shrine housing many idols, visited by pilgrims from across western Arabia.

kempten.s: Kempten is a city on the Iller in the Allgäu, Bavaria, and one of the oldest towns in Germany, on the site of Roman Cambodunum. For centuries it was divided between the Catholic prince-abbey of Kempten and the Protestant Free Imperial City, until both passed to Bavaria in…

kamien-pomorski.s: Kamień Pomorski, in German Cammin, is a town near the mouth of the Oder in north-western Poland. From the late 12th century it was the seat of the bishops of Pomerania, whose Romanesque-Gothic cathedral survives.

kolobrzeg.s: Kołobrzeg, in German Kolberg, is a port and spa town on the Baltic coast of north-western Poland. Bolesław I made it the seat of one of Poland's first bishoprics in 1000, and from 1248 it belonged to the bishops of Cammin.

koszalin.s: Koszalin, in German Köslin, is a city in West Pomeranian Voivodeship, north-western Poland, near the Baltic coast. Granted town rights in 1266, it was a main residence of the bishops of Cammin, who ruled it as part of their secular territory.

kampen.s: Kampen is a town in the Dutch province of Overijssel, near the mouth of the IJssel. In the 14th and 15th centuries it was one of the wealthiest towns of the northern Netherlands, a Hanseatic port trading with the Baltic and England.

karytaina.s: Karytaina is a village in Arcadia in the central Peloponnese, dominated by a castle on a crag above the Alpheios river. It was the seat of a barony of the Principality of Achaea, and its castle was built around 1254 by Geoffrey of Bruyères, hero of the Chronicle of the Morea.

kothen.s: Köthen is a town in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, between the Elbe and the Saale. From 1603 to 1847 it was the residence of the princes, later dukes, of Anhalt-Köthen.

kapellmeister.s: Kapellmeister is a German title for the director of music at a princely court or church, originally the leader of a chapel's musicians. In the baroque period a Kapellmeister composed, rehearsed and directed music for services, ceremonies and entertainments.

kruje.s: Krujë is a town in north-central Albania, on a mountainside above the coastal plain. In the late 12th century it was the centre of Arbanon, the first Albanian principality.

kokcha-river.s: The Kokcha is a river in Badakhshan in north-eastern Afghanistan, a left tributary of the Panj, the upper course of the Amu Darya. Rising in the Hindu Kush, it flows north past Fayzabad.

kirillo-belozersky-monastery.s: The Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery is a monastery at Kirillov in Vologda Oblast, Russia, founded in 1397 by the monk Cyril of White Lake on the shore of the Siverskoye lake. Favoured by the grand princes and tsars, it became one of the largest landowners in Russia and a centre…

karachay-cherkessia.s: Karachay-Cherkessia is a republic of the Russian Federation in the north-western Caucasus, with its capital at Cherkessk. It is home mainly to the Turkic Karachays, the Cherkess (Circassians), the Abazins and Russians.

kursk.s: Kursk is a city in south-western Russia on the Seym river, first mentioned in 1032. It was a town of the Chernigov lands on the edge of the steppe and was destroyed in the Mongol invasion of 1240.

koppany.s: Koppány was a Hungarian chieftain of the Árpád dynasty who ruled lands in Somogy, south of Lake Balaton. On Grand Prince Géza's death in 997 he claimed the succession by the old custom of seniority and sought to marry Géza's widow, but he was defeated near Veszprém by Géza's…

kabardians.s: The Kabardians are the eastern branch of the Circassians, living chiefly in Kabardino-Balkaria in the North Caucasus. From the 15th century their princes ruled the plains of Kabarda along the Terek and its tributaries and held sway over neighbouring mountain peoples.

kostroma.s: Kostroma is a city in Russia on the Volga, at the mouth of the Kostroma river, north-east of Moscow. Founded in the 12th century, traditionally by Yuri Dolgoruky, it was the seat of an appanage principality of the Vladimir-Suzdal lands before passing to Moscow in the 14th…

kusel.s: Kusel is a small town in the Western Palatinate, Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany. Nearby stands the ruined Lichtenberg Castle, one of the largest castle ruins in Germany, which gave its name to the Principality of Lichtenberg, a Saxe-Coburg exclave from 1816 to 1834.

karigaila.s: Karigaila was a son of Grand Duke Algirdas of Lithuania and Uliana of Tver and a brother of Jogaila. He held Mstislavl as an appanage in the 1380s and fought for Jogaila against the Teutonic Order and against Vytautas.

kraft-ernst-prince-of-oettingen-wallerst.s: Kraft Ernst was Count, from 1774 Prince, of Oettingen-Wallerstein in the Ries of Swabia. A devoted patron of music, he built up one of the finest court orchestras in Germany, with Antonio Rosetti among its members, and he collected books and manuscripts for the family library,…

kideksha.s: Kideksha is a village on the Nerl river near Suzdal, Russia. Its Church of Saints Boris and Gleb, built in 1152 at a residence of Yuri Dolgoruky, is among the oldest white-stone churches of north-eastern Rus' and marks the beginning of the architecture of Vladimir-Suzdal.

karl-gunther-prince-of-schwarzburg-sonde.s: Karl Günther was the last Prince of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen, reigning from 1880 until his death. A conservative ruler of a small Thuringian state within the German Empire, he died without children, and the principality passed in personal union to his kinsman Günther Victor…

kasogs.s: Kasogs was the name used in the medieval Rus' chronicles for the Circassians, the Adyghe peoples of the north-western Caucasus. They lived near the Rus' principality of Tmutarakan and served in its armies.

kosice.s: Košice, in Hungarian Kassa, is the second-largest city of Slovakia, in the east of the country. In the Kingdom of Hungary it was a leading royal free town and the chief city of Upper Hungary, with the Gothic Cathedral of St Elizabeth.

kuruc.s: Kuruc was the name given to the armed anti-Habsburg rebels of Royal Hungary between 1671 and 1711. Drawn from Protestant nobles, lesser gentry, haiduks and peasants, they fought against Habsburg absolutism and religious persecution, first under Imre Thököly and later in…

kanine.s: Kaninë is a village and medieval castle on a hill above Vlorë in south-western Albania. The fortress, with late antique origins, guarded the port of Vlorë and was held in turn by Byzantium, the Serbian Empire, the lords of Valona and, from 1417, the Ottomans.

kotorosl.s: The Kotorosl is a river in Yaroslavl Oblast, Russia, about 130 kilometres long, flowing from Lake Nero near Rostov to join the Volga at Yaroslavl. The city of Yaroslavl was founded on the headland at its mouth in the early 11th century, and the river linked the old Rostov…

kennebec-river.s: The Kennebec River flows about 270 km from Moosehead Lake to the Atlantic in Maine, United States. The short-lived Popham Colony was planted at its mouth in 1607, and Plymouth Colony ran a fur-trading post on it at Cushnoc, now Augusta.

kittery-maine.s: Kittery is a town in southern Maine, United States, at the mouth of the Piscataqua River opposite Portsmouth, New Hampshire. Settled in the 1620s and incorporated in 1647, it is the oldest incorporated town in Maine.

kapunda.s: Kapunda is a town north of Adelaide in South Australia, founded after copper was found there in 1842. Its mine, opened in 1844, was the first successful metal mine in Australia, and together with the Burra mine it lifted South Australia out of its early financial crisis.

kazys-skirpa.s: Kazys Škirpa was a Lithuanian army officer and diplomat, envoy in Berlin, who founded the Lithuanian Activist Front there in 1940 after the Soviet occupation of Lithuania. He was named prime minister of the provisional government proclaimed during the June Uprising of 1941,…

kim-gu.s: Kim Gu was a Korean independence leader who headed the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea in China for much of the period from the late 1920s to 1945. He organised the Korean Patriotic Organisation, whose members included Yun Bong-gil, and created the Korean…

korean-liberation-army.s: The Korean Liberation Army was the armed force of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea, founded in Chongqing in September 1940 with Chinese Nationalist support. Its members fought alongside Chinese and British forces against Japan, including in Burma, and…

komotini.s: Komotini is a city in Western Thrace in north-eastern Greece, capital of the region of Eastern Macedonia and Thrace. Under Ottoman rule, as Gümülcine, it had a mainly Muslim population, and in 1913 it was the seat of the short-lived Provisional Government of Western Thrace.

king-of-battle.s: The King of Battle (Akkadian šar tamḫāri) is a Mesopotamian legend in which Sargon of Akkad marches to Purushanda in Anatolia to protect Akkadian merchants from its king, Nur-Daggal. Known from a copy found at Amarna in Egypt, dating to the 14th century BCE, and from Assyrian…

kyaukse.s: Kyaukse is a town and district south of Mandalay in central Myanmar, on a plain watered by the Zawgyi and Panlaung rivers. Its weirs and canals, among the oldest irrigation works in the country, made it the rice granary of the dry zone, and the Burmans who settled there in the…

karen-people.s: The Karen are a group of related peoples speaking Karenic languages, living mainly in the hills of south-eastern Myanmar along the Thai border, with communities in Thailand. Many became Christians through 19th-century Baptist missions.
